Economy—Reports
1. CHRIS BISHOP (National) to the Minister of Finance: What recent reports has
he received about what progress the Government is making to support more jobs and
higher incomes?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the  Minister
of Finance : I have seen several reports, particularly since this House last sat before
Christmas, confirming that the growing economy is continuing to support more jobs and
higher incomes. For example, Statistics New Zealand last week reported that in the past
year another 80,000 jobs were created across New Zealand. The labour market
participation rate increased to a record 69.7 percent, and unemployment, at 5.7 percent,
is lower than i n most other developed economies. Average weekly wages rose 2.5
percent in the calendar year of 2014, compared with consumer price inflation of just 0.8
percent in the same period, and we also now know that mortgage interest rates will stay
lower for longe r. So the growing economy is helping New Zealanders in many ways,
but, of course, there is always more work to do to lock in those gains over the longer
term.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: In light of forecasts of further strong economic growth, what is the
outlook for inflation and interest rates?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Both inflation and interest rate pressures are low, and they
are expected to remain that way now for the foreseeable future. The Reserve Bank noted
in its latest official cash rate review that low global inflation and the impact of sharply
lower oil prices will continue to increase New Zealand households’ purchasing power
and will lower the cost of doing business. Headline annual inflation is expected to be
below the bank’s 1 to 3 percent target band through 2015 and could become negative
for a period, before moving back towards 2 percent. In the current circumstances the
Reserve Bank expects to keep the official cash rate on hold for some time. Of course,
1536 Oral Questions 12 Feb 2015
that will be welcomed b y both homeowners and businesses. Future interest rate
adjustments will, of course, depend on the emerging flow of economic data.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: According to the official statistics, how do the latest average wage
increases compare with inflation, and how does this compare with historical
movements?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The quarterly employment survey, which successive
Governments have used to set New Zealand superannuation, for example, shows that
average weekly wages rose 2.5 percent in the 12 months to 31 December. As I
mentioned earlier, this is above the annual inflation rate of just 0.8 percent. In the past 5
years, average wages have increased by 15 percent, and they are forecast to keep rising
faster than the cost of living. This contrasts with the position in 2008, when wages were
struggling to keep pace with consumer price annual inflation of more than 5 percent.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: What policy measures has the Government announced that will
distribute dividends from the growing economy to New Zealand families and children?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: A number of important changes will take effect in the next
few months that will help families and children. For example, from 1 April, paid
parental leave will increase by 2 weeks to 16 weeks and by another 2 weeks from 1
April of next year; the parental tax credit will rise from $150 a week to $220 a week,
and the entitlement will increase from 8 weeks to 10 weeks; and the Government’s new
HomeStart scheme will help around 90,000 Kiwis into their first home over the next 5
years. From 1 July, children under 13 will have access to free general practitioner visits
and free prescriptions, and the average ACC levy for a private motor vehicle will fall by
around $130 a year. These are just some of the policies this Government is introducing
to support families, on the back of a strong economy and good fiscal management.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Can the Minister please tell us by just how much the wage gap
with Australia has grown since his Government promised to close it in 2008?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I do not have those numbers to hand, but I can tell the
member—and this contributes to that explanation for those numbers —that more and
more people are moving to this side of the Tasman rather than to Australia. In fact, for
the first time since 1990 —the first time since 1990 —more people are moving from
Australia to here than from New Zealand—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was very
specific: how much has the wage gap with Australia grown? There was no politics in it.
If the Minister does not know, he should just sit down.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is my job to adjudicate when an answer goes on for too
long. The Minister answered immediately by saying that he did not have the
information with him, and that is acceptable. He then did give quite a long answer,
which was not adding information to the question that was asked by the member, and I
accept that, but it is still my job and not Mr Clark’s job to judge the length of an answer.
Primary Growth Partnership—Overseas Interests and Intellectual Property
2. RICHARD PROSSER (NZ First) to the Minister for Primary Industries: Does
he believe the Primary Growth Partnership provides value for money to taxpayers?
Hon JO GOODHEW (Associate Minister for Primary Industries)  on behalf of
the Minister for Primary Industries : Yes. As the member will be aware, last year an
independent report by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research estimated that
the Primary Growth Partnership will add $6.4 billion per annum to New Zealand’s
economy by 2025. The report further concluded that the Primary Growth Partnership
has the potential to achieve an additional $4.7 billion per annum by 2025 if all the
research and development is successful, the aspirat ional stretch of the Primary Growth
Partnership programmes is achieved, and the innovations are widely taken up. That is
12 Feb 2015 Oral Questions 1537
why my answer is yes. This makes a 30 -year benefit-cost ratio for Government funding
of 1:32. That confirms what great value the Primary Growth Partnership programme is.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: How much of the $322 million of taxpayers’ funds committed to
the Primary Growth Partnership by the Crown has gone to overseas-owned companies?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: I do not have an answer to that question. It has a level of
technical detail that I would have preferred to be laid down in the primary question.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: How much has gone to the following partners: PGG Wrightson,
which is now majority Chinese- owned; the majority Japanese- owned ANZCO Foods;
and Norske Skog Tasman, owned by Norwegian and other overseas interests?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: What I can tell the member is that the benefits to New
Zealand, as have been calculated by the independent report of the New Zealand Institute
of Economic Research, are considerable. This country has many businesses that have
some capital input from overseas, but it is the New Zealand economy that benefits
significantly from the money that is investe d into quality programmes that will achieve
great benefits in primary industries for New Zealand.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Who owns the intellectual property of the programmes: the New
Zealand taxpayer, who funds them through the partnership, or the private entities, some
of which are overseas-owned?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: The recent report by the Office of the Auditor -General
identified to us that intellectual property and the identification of the benefits of that are
important parts o f the clarification that the Ministry for Primary Industries needs to
continue working on. We have taken that feedback from the office on board, and that
will be the case.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Given that answer, will the Minister now give the  House an
assurance that changes will be made to the Primary Growth Partnership scheme to
ensure that the New Zealand taxpayer will benefit directly from the ownership of
intellectual property; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: I reiterate my earlier answer to the member, and I also add to
that that there have been learnings since the beginning of this significant programme of
benefits to primary industries in New Zealand —an exciting programme that looks to
deliver great benefits to New Zeal and. The Office of the Auditor -General’s report is
largely positive, but it does point us to some areas where we can improve. That is not a
surprise, but it is an encouragement to the Ministry for Primary Industries.
Skycity Convention Centre—Proposed Government Funding
3. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Finance:
In light of his comments that a taxpayer bailout is his “ least preferred ” option, how
much is he prepared to spend to save the SkyCity deal?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the  Minister
of Finance : I would like to simply point the member to the answer given by my
colleague the Minister for Economic Development yesterday to an exceedingly similar
question: “I have been clear all the way through that our least preferred option is to
provide any funding to Skycity for the convention centre. We are in the process of
discussions, and I am not prepared to conduct those discussions in the public domain, as
that would undermine our position.”

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of that answer, when he said in the House on 12
November 2013 that for a “little, if any, investment by taxpayers,” New Zealanders
would get an international -standard convention centre, how big did he envisage the
“little” investment was going to be, and did that also include an international standard
that was not an eyesore?
1538 Oral Questions 12 Feb 2015

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, to the latter part of the question. In terms of the first
part I refer the member to the primary answer to the primary question. But the clear
position of the Government, the Minis ter for Economic Development, the Minister of
Finance, and the Prime Minister is that actually our least preferred option is to provide
any funding to Skycity. However, there have, of course, been other positions this week.
In fact, when asked whether the Government should contribute funds to the convention
centre, one response was: “You could probably say, you know, for the overall benefit,
yes.”, and speaking of “little” that was one Andrew Little on Newstalk ZB.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can he assu re the New Zealand public that any decisions around
potentially giving millions of dollars of taxpayers’ money to Skycity will not have been
affected by the tens of thousands of dollars Skycity has donated to the National Party,
such as the $60,000 donation recorded in 2005?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In so far as there may be some ministerial responsibility, the Hon
Steven Joyce.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure of the ministerial responsibility, but I think
the answer would be yes anyway.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of his comments yesterday, when did he advise all other
Ministers that a taxpayer bailout of Skycity would require a cut to their budgets to
stump up for cash for a business that made a $66.6 million profit in the last 6 months?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the member is actually mischaracterising the
Minister’s comments yesterday, but nevertheless it is clear that it is the Government’s
preference that our least preferred option is to provide any  funding to Skycity. No
proposal has been received from the Minister for Economic Development to the
Minister of Finance, at least that I am aware of—and I think I may have been aware of it
if it had occurred—and in the meantime we will just see how it goes.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Point of order, the Hon Annette King.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Do not sound so weary, Mr Speaker. This is a really good point
of order. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am looking forward to it with —[Interruption] Order!
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Well, a second point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, well—[Interruption] Order! We will deal with the first point of
order first, which I am looking forward to with anticipation and excitement.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Yes, Mr Speaker. I have taken your advice in terms of very tight
questions. My question asked when the Minist er of Finance advised all Ministers that
there would need to be a taxpayer bailout if they were required to provide money to
Skycity, and the Minister did not answer that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: He did. He disputed that he had had those discussions with t he
Ministers, as I understood the answer. In my opinion he definitely addressed that
question.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Will he guarantee today that he will not support further
gambling concessions to Skycity to save the deal?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government has confirmed that there will not be
further concessions in any further law changes.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How many hip operations could be undertaken and how many
State houses could be built for the $128 mi llion dollars that Skycity is demanding from
the taxpayers, and would it not be of more benefit to New Zealanders to invest it in
them rather than in a multinational company that is making huge profits?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member presu mes way too much in her statement and
it is highly hypothetical. But if she is concerned about that, I would talk to her own
12 Feb 2015 Oral Questions 1539
leader, who actually was on the radio this week saying funds should be contributed to
Skycity. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAK ER
items.text: Order! The interjection level coming from both sides is now
unacceptable.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If the Prime Minister will not listen to him—the Minister of
Finance—will he listen to the 22,000 New Zealanders who in just the past 1 day h ave
signed Labour’s petition opposing a taxpayer bailout of the Skycity deal?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I need to point out to the member that the Government’s
position is entirely consistent. The Prime Minister has made it clear that it is his least
preferred option to provide any funding to Skycity. The Minister of Finance has made it
clear that our least preferred option is to provide any funding to Skycity. The Minister
for Economic Development has been saying since December last year that ou r least
preferred option is to provide any funding to Skycity. I appreciate that on close
examination those three statements may sound very different, but I have done some
analysis in my office by placing them side by side and they are, in fact, the same.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he prepared to match the contribution to the Skycity bailout
raised yesterday from the public, who showed what they thought of the Government’s
idea by donating $41.20, two bottles of water, and a lime Fruit Burst lolly?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would point out that, as we have been clear about all the
way through, negotiations are continuing. Our least preferred option is to provide any
funding to Skycity. It is fair to say that the member’s leader is  well ahead of her in that
he signalled the other day that he would be prepared to give more than the amount of
money that the member’s question has just raised.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I do not think that the
member heard my question or understood it, and I am very happy to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No. I am sure he did hear it. It was whether the Minister
gave a guarantee that he would match the public contribution. He clearly said he was
not prepared to give that guarantee, because it is still in the stage of negotiation.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I seek leave to table a transcript of Andrew Little with
Larry Williams on Newstalk ZB—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Transcripts are freely available to members if they want to
get them.
Skycity Convention Centre—Television New Zealand Land
4. DENISE ROCHE (Green)  to the Minister for Economic Development : What
advice did officials provi de about how much more valuable to SkyCity the TVNZ land
sold to it for the siting of a convention centre was, once that land was used as the site of
a hotel?

items.speaker: Hon STEV EN JOYCE
items.text: The first thing I
would point out is that the site, of course, has not yet been used for a hotel. Negotiations
are ongoing regarding the final layout, cost, and size of the convention centre complex.
With regard to the plans submitted to Auckland Council by Skycity at the end of last
year, I am advised that there is a potential benefit to Skycity of a change in location, but,
as the final form of the convention centre is still being negotiated, I cannot at this stage
provide an estimate of that benefit. But I have been clear to our negotiators that I would
expect that anything that gave that benefit to Skycity would be a cost that they would
need to take account of.

items.speaker: Denise Roche
items.text: I raise a point of  order, Mr Speaker. My question was on notice, and
it specifically asked about the advice that was given about the change in the land value,
not about any other sort of advice that he has had since. It was about the advice that he
received before the deal took place.
1540 Oral Questions 12 Feb 2015

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, as I interpreted the Minister’s answer, he said there could
well be an increased value because of subsequent use, but it was impossible at this stage
to put a figure on it until the plans were finalised as to what that site would totally be
used for. I think that the question has been adequately addressed, and I suggest that if
the member wants to take the matter further, tease it out now with good supplementary
questions.

items.speaker: Denise Roche
items.text: Why did he not work out how much more the deal  was worth to
Skycity with the hotel on Television New Zealand (TVNZ) land before the deal was
signed, given that officials said it made the deal much more valuable to Skycity?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure what the member is driving a t, because,
actually, there has been a proposal for the hotel to be on a different site —and I would
stress that Skycity already had its own site for a hotel it is basically proposing to shift
from one part of the site to another part of the site —and until that proposal was made, it
would have been difficult to anticipate the need for putting a value on a proposal of that
nature. I have been quite clear to the member in the answer to the primary question that
I believe there probably is a value out of that, and that that value should be accounted
for in any subsequent negotiations.

items.speaker: Denise Roche
items.text: How is it that his deal allowed Skycity to acquire a prime piece of
central Auckland real estate, discounted at taxpayer expense, and somehow a year later
Skycity comes back asking for even more handouts?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am sorry; the member is incorrect. I am not sure where
she got the idea there was any sort of discount, but, actually, as I understand it, Skycity
has paid somethi ng in the order of —I do not know —$16 million or something, which
was a commercial valuation on the site, firstly. I think TVNZ is currently using the
money to renovate its facilities in Auckland, so it obviously got the value from it. And
in terms of where  the hotel goes on the overall site, that is something that we would
negotiate with them in terms of any value they would obtain from that. So I just do not
know what the member sees as the massive issue here.

items.speaker: Denise Roche
items.text: Did the Minister’s lawyers advise not to include clause 11.47 of the
convention centre agreement, which effectively allows Skycity to plan a bigger and
flasher centre to renegotiate the whole deal; if so, why did he include it?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am sorry; I think the member is incorrect. There was a
deal that was done for a convention centre at the value of $402 million. That is finally
confirmed at the time—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: That’s not what you told the public at the time.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —listen to me —a construction agreement is signed, at
which point the concessions that are in return for the convention centre would come into
force. Prior to that time, either party could withdraw from it. What Skyc ity is saying is
that it has got a bit more expensive and it is worried about that, and it wants to negotiate
with the Crown. What we have said is that we will listen to them and that we will have
the discussions, but that any money would be our least pref erred option. That is the
whole of the week, I do believe, in the media.

items.speaker: Denise Roche
items.text: Is he embarrassed that he negotiated a deal that allowed Skycity to
walk away with a large chunk of prime public land for its own hotel and to completely
change the size and cost of the so-called free convention centre.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am sorry; much of what the member is saying in her
question I just completely disagree with. The simple thing the member needs to
understand in this is that that company already had some land set aside for a hotel. It has
proposed to shift the location of that hotel as part of its latest proposed facility for the
consent, so that, actually, the convention centre works a bit better on the site. We will
12 Feb 2015 Oral Questions 1541
make a judgment on that, and assess the value of that, and that will form part of any
further discussions.

items.speaker: Denise Roche
items.text: Why will he not just admit that he and Mr Key have been played by
much better gamblers, and it is time to fold ‘em and walk away?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure that it is news that the Greens oppose a
convention centre in Auckland, but obviously we will choose to disagree, as I think we
have since roughly 2009.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Does he hav e any absolute and specified negotiating bottom lines
beyond which he will walk away from the convention centre deal?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As I said to the member yesterday, I am not prepared to
conduct the negotiations in public, because t hat would actually make the Crown’s
position weaker, and I would prefer to have a stronger position and have the option of
conducting those discussions and then reporting back the result of those discussions to
the House.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: I  raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am just asking for your
assistance. I think the member has misunderstood my question, which was whether he
has any—it was a yes or no. I do not want the nature of them—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will r esume his seat. The member’s question
was whether there were any bottom lines, and the Minister clearly, in answering, said he
was not prepared to reveal his position on a negotiation that is still proceeding.
Cricket World Cup 2015—Benefits
5. MATT DOOCEY (National —Waimakariri) to the Minister for Sport and

items.speaker: Recreation
items.text: What benefits does he expect to be delivered by the Government ’s support
for the Cricket World Cup?
Tonight’s opening ceremony for the International Cricket Council Cricket World Cup in
North Hagley Park, Ch ristchurch, is the start of a wonderful 6- week festival of
international cricket. The global television audience is over 1 billion, with an expected
30,000 visitors to New Zealand and 239,000 visitor nights. It is expected to inject
around $50 million into the New Zealand economy. There will be ongoing benefits for
New Zealand through the raised international profile that the tournament brings to this
country. Three hundred thousand tickets have been sold for games in New Zealand, so
be in quick.

items.speaker: Matt Doocey
items.text: What has been planned for the opening ceremony of the tournament?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The opening ceremony will be free to attend,
with live music and several enormous games of backyard cricket. It is going t o be great.
The ceremony—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am going to ask the Minister to start his answer again. I
cannot hear it because of the level of noise from my left.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The ceremony wi ll be free to attend, with live
music and several enormous games of backyard cricket. It is going to be a great
ceremony. That ceremony and the opening game will help show the world that
Christchurch is open for business and provide Cantabrians with a grea t opportunity to
show their support for the Black Caps and the tournament. Frankly, it is time the Labour
Party backed this tournament.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Is it correct that the shot involving the Prime Minister for the
opening ceremony had to be reshot six times because he kept on dropping the ball?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In so far as there may potentially be ministerial responsibility, I will
ask the Minister.
1542 Oral Questions 12 Feb 2015

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: No; as per usual, he hi t it out of the park. But
what I can say is correct is that although Mr Mallard bags the Cricket World Cup, he is
quite prepared to accept the invitations and even wear the tie.

items.speaker: Matt Doocey
items.text: What leverage and legacy benefits will be provided by co -hosting the
tournament?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The Government has been focused on a
coordinated leverage and legacy programme, including helping New Zealand businesses
develop international connections , and showcasing New Zealand industry, culture, and
expertise, to further drive trade and visitation opportunities. There is also an educational
programme for primary and intermediate schools called Cricket Smart. The Cricket
World Cup is a huge opportunity for all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Clayton Mitchell
items.text: Does he believe that Kiwis without Sky TV should get to see all
of the Cricket World Cup matches live considering that $5 million of taxpayers’ money
has gone into funding the event, yet only a selection of games w ill be available free to
air; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I have not had a single email on that issue, and
I think New Zealanders are just really thrilled that we have got this tournament coming
to New Zealand. There  are still tickets available and there are going to be key games
shown on Prime Television, free to air.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: In view of all this, can the Minister think of any sporting
tournaments or ceremonies where it is not the role of the Government to fund with
taxpayer money?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I am sure there are some, but I am not going to
get into it here.
Primary Growth Partnership—Growth
6. Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) to the Minister
for Primary Industries: Does he have confidence in his department?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: on behalf of
the Minister for Primary Industries : Yes. In particular, I have confidence in the
support that the Ministry for Primary Industries provides to all in the primary sector. As
an example, today, a medium-scale adverse event has been declared across most of the
east coast of the South Island. There are still tough times ahead for many farmers, but
farmers are resilient, and today’s announcement confirms that this Government and the
Ministry for Primary Industries will back them through this.
Hon Damien O ’Connor: How can he have confidence in his department when the
Auditor-General has found that his officials could not yet show what the $322 million
committed and the $129 m illion spent so far on the Primary Growth Partnership have
achieved; and of the six programmes fully audited, it said “It is too soon to observe any
economic benefit.”?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Well, the Minister has confidence in the Primary Growt h
Partnership, but also in understanding that this is a long process. The Auditor -General’s
report showed that the reporting that is currently under way could be made more simple
for the average reader in the street , and we have certainly taken that on board. But I
remind the member that there are not only detailed websites, quarterly reports, a regular
newsletter, an annual expo, presence at the Fieldays, programme steering groups,
quarterly progress reporting, and annual plans and audits to show the publi c of New
Zealand what they will get over the long term. As I have already explained today, the
New Zealand Institute of Economic Research  report, out to 2025, shows the billions of
dollars that will actually be available to the economy of New Zealand, but this is a long-

Social Housing—Reform
7. ALFRED NGARO (National) to the Minister for Social Housing : What recent
commitments has the Government made to improving social housing?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The Prime Minister
recently announced a comprehensive social housing reform package that will ensure
that more people in need get access to social housing. For too long Governments have
focused on the number of houses they owned rather than how many people they are
housing and what ki nds of lives they are leading. We will ensure there are more social
housing places than there are now, and that is starting with an extra 3,000 income -
related rent subsidies over the next 3 years.

items.text: Why is the Government focusing on tenants rather than the number of

items.text: Because tenants care about having a roof over their heads

housing providers are well established and already provide around 5,000 social houses
around the country. We will grow the community housing sector by selling 1,000 to

change means that community housing providers now have a guaranteed income stream
from the Government that will help them grow and gives their tenants access to housing
help previously given only exclusively to State housing tenants.

1550 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT
Debate resumed from 11 February.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: What a fantastic
country we live in, and what a fantastic bunch of New Zealanders we have got in it. We
have just had a fantastic summer. We have got so many things on track. We have more
work to do, but we are heading in the right direction.
Let us look at the fact that we have got one of the highest economic growth rates in
the OECD. Employment is growing, with 80,000 new jobs created last year. Fewer
people are dependent on welfare. The 2014 December quarter shows that benefit
numbers are at a 6 -year low. We have fewer teens having babies than we have had in
the last 42 years. We are seeing our roads being upgraded. More New Zealanders are
getting the operations they need. We are seeing our construction centre booming. More
houses are getting built. That is the reality of the direction this country is going in.
However, if you listen to the Opposition, you would think it is all doom and gloom.
It might be in their lives—it might be in their lives. That might be how it is for Labour. I
mean, if you do not like the person you are sitting next to and if only four of you
actually voted for the leader that you have got, then it might be that it is a bit doom and
gloom. But that is not the reality of the New Zealand that we are living in today. It is not
the reality of what we are seeing in the lives that people are living, in the optimism they
have, and in the belief not only that through their own hard work things are getting
better but also that the future looks pretty damned bright.
This year we have announced, though, a fundamental policy within the housing and
social housing sector so that we can continue to make sure we are addressing the needs
of New Zealanders who really need help the most. For years we have seen Labour
trying to define whether or not New Zealanders are getting their housing needs met by
counting the number of houses that the State owns —full stop. There is no consideration
given to the lives that those people are leading and the support services that they mig ht
actually need. There is no consideration given to whether or not there might actually be
someone better than the State who could do a better job for them. Let us just count the
houses, tick that box, and we have done our job, which, by the way, would ge t kind of
interesting in itself if we did decide to go down that track, because Labour had only
59,000 houses back in 2004, and we now lease up to 69,000—but we will not let the
facts get in the way of Labour’s doom and gloom story.
So we announced changes  that mean, fundamentally, that New Zealanders will have
more choice, more availability of social housing, and better services wrapped around
them as individuals, and we are growing a community housing sector that  is, quite
frankly, awesome —awesome; absolutely incredible. There is someone in this House
who agrees with me. You heard me in question time today. It is quite exciting. Phil
Twyford himself —yes, Phil Twyford himself —goes out there and says to the
community housing sector: “We are committed to your  members having access to the
income-related rents subsidy, to capital grants, and to stock transfer.” Well tick, tick,
tick—that is actually Government policy. Thanks for the support, Phil Twyford. Good
on you! But, members, you would be mistaken if you thought that he was actually being
consistent and that what he said to them is what he actually believed. That is not true.
Just this week —in fact, just today —we got a crowdfunding email to Labour
supporters. It says: “Can you imagine John Key’s face if he opened the newspaper next
week and saw a full page ad highlighting how many New Zealanders are against State
house sell-offs? He would be straight on the phone to his Ministers. Through the power
of crowdfunding we can make that happen. We can put an ad in the paper—if only you
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1551
can all give us a couple of pennies, because we do not even actually have the money to
put an ad in the paper.” So poor Labour, guys —it is heading for a by -election it cannot
afford; it is flip -flopping on policy. It goes out to the community sector saying one
thing, because it wants them onside, but then it actually goes out with its little bucket
because it cannot even afford an ad in the newspaper, which it thinks is going to make
John Key sit up and take notice. What Labour does not get, though, ladies and
gentlemen, is that this is actually about people. So it is people who have often been
stuck in pretty dysfunctional situations, in pretty lousy housing. Let us all remember
what Labour has turned around and said repeatedly: “As l ong as we can tick the box of
the number of houses that the State owns, then we are doing a good enough job by those
people.” We do not think we are.
When I look at organisations that take women and their children who have come out
of pretty hideous domest ic violence circumstances, they can put them in a safe house;
get them temporarily set up; move them somewhere where they can stay longer term—
where they will need to spend quite a bit of time to get through the trauma they have
been in; work with them to help them into jobs; keep their kids in school, which is what
is actually needed to put the sort of safety and security around them they need; give
them hope and ambition so they can save and can get our fantastic home loan starts,
which are coming up very  shortly; and then see them actually get into affordable
housing. It is called being ambitious. It is called actually believing in people and their
ability, and more so in those organisations that can wrap that kind of support around
them for a long period of time.
Do not underestimate the effects of having the income -related rents subsidies going
to community housing providers. It gives them a certainty of income for the year. It
gives them the ability to partner with others who have equity so that they can borrow off
it. It means they can look at homeownership for some of those who are at the tougher
end of the scale, because they can actually walk them through the housing continuum,
which can be pretty tough, as we know, for people who are just trying to get a foot on
the property ladder. Having that income -related rent subsidy —which, in my opinion,
was so arrogantly designed only for those in State houses —opened up to a much wider
and diverse sector makes a huge difference.
Think of those with drug and al cohol addictions who do get into programmes for
long periods of time. They leave those rehabilitation programmes and they need
somewhere safe and secure to live that will give them the bridge that will then take them
through and into their own security, wh ether that be into a rental or actually into buying
their own home. It makes sense that they have the support of an organisation that is
community-based and that knows them, knows the place they live in, and is able to
work with them over a period of time. And we are in favour of that —we want to
support that. I make no apologies. In fact, I stand here proudly to say that we will
support the community housing sector to grow, and we will sell some of our houses to it
so that it actually has another kind of ba se to work from. I think it could do it, at the
very least, as well as the Government —and certainly Housing New Zealand does —and
in some cases it could do it a lot better because those providers can really get in and
work over a long period of time.
The other thing about the income-related rent subsidies is that there will be times—as
the Ministry of Social Development now does with that structure of whom they give it
to—when they will say: “Here is a mum and her children who have come out of a
domestic vio lence place, or with alcohol or drug issues, who actually need some
certainty of tenure. We want her to be in the same house for a minimum of 12 years, and
we will go out there and bid accordingly —and actually pay the cost—to ensure that she
has certainty of tenure.” Yes? So we will pay extra. We will pay for more support
1552 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
around her to make sure that she is in a home where the kids can get into school. We
will put the right kind of social work and services around her, and actually see a
certainty of tenure.
You know, these are the kinds of innovative things that we can do in a true
partnership with community housing providers, not the rubbish we have heard and the
lip service of a member who stands up and says one thing to the community housing
sector and th en turns around and says another thing to the media about what he truly
believes its capability is to service people in their own communities, which they are the
specialists to do.
So we back community housing providers. We believe in them. We know that there
is a long way to go for us to see them playing a larger part, but we will put the money
behind them, we will back them in both our contracts with them, and we will also make
sure that they are serviced and can keep an absolute focus on the tenants and the people
who need it most.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Kia ora tātou and welcome
back, everybody, for the Parliament of 2015, and I just want to say that it has been a
wonderful, long, hot summer break. In fact, it has been an “f” of a summer break for me
and the Labour Party: it has been family, it has been fun, and it has been food—food for
the body and food for the mind. And I have to tell the members opposite that the “f”
story continues, because Labour has come back and we are fighting fit. We are full of
fortitude, and the winds of good fortune are now blowing our way.
You know when you have got the Government on the run, and you know it because
the Prime Ministe r’s speech was more about the Leader of the Opposition than it was
about his own achievements, his own vision, or his goals. He spent 10 minutes slagging
off Andrew Little with a whole series of prepared jokes and pathetic little insults,
combined, I have to say, with a number of malicious fabrications. Well, Andrew Little
scares the hell out of John Key and he is also scaring the hell out of the National Party,
and I can tell you why. It is because its polling will be telling it the same thing as ours
is, the same as TV3’s is, and the same as the New Zealand Herald’s is. It is saying that
Andrew Little is making Labour relevant again. He is connecting with New Zealanders.
His favourability is rising rapidly. Yes, those members are afraid. They have had it t oo
easy for too long.
His message is one of straight talking—his no-frills approach of going to the heart of
the problem and having the guts to talk about the real issues. It is not hiding behind the
window dressing and the candyfloss that you get from the Prime Minister. Andrew
Little is talking about jobs and housing, unfairness, and the Government’s double -speak
and its arrogance. You know, New Zealanders like the cut of his jib. They like the cut of
his jib, and increasingly they are comparing it with the jibber -jabber of John Key —the
jibber-jabber that we get daily in this House that does not make sense. I am having great
difficulty understanding anything the man says these days. Well, John Key, we are
coming after you because we are going right to you r heartland. Andrew Little,
combined with a number of our members, is right out there amongst the businesses of
New Zealand. You know what they are saying? They are saying that this is a breath of
fresh air. We have got politicians willing to listen. They are willing to engage, and
businesses are saying: “We want to engage with Labour because this is a tired
Government we have now got.”
When I came back into the House for the first day, on Tuesday, all bright -eyed and
bushy-tailed, wanting to be back in here debating with the members opposite, what did I
see? I saw some dull eyes, some weary, uninterested Ministers, and some very bored
backbenchers. They were far too important to be wasting their time sitting around in this
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1553
Parliament. We get dismissive answ ers. We get evasive behaviour. It is a third- term
Government, and it has got “third-term-itis”.
I went through the Prime Minister’s statement. I was looking to be uplifted by the
power of his words. I was looking for his vision, and a programme and an age nda that
would take New Zealand forward to address some of those issues that are closing in on
us rapidly. What did I find? I found a skite sheet from a dirty, flash Government. That is
what my mother would call it—a dirty, flash Government. You see, the m embers are
flash on the outside. There are plenty of photos of them, selfies at every occasion,
wearing the appropriate clothes for whatever it is, whether they are at the cricket or the
rugby or the Big Gay Out. Appearances, schmoozing, and endless report s and
committees—that is the dirty, flash Government. It is flash on the outside, but just look
inside this Government. It is enmeshed in sleazy deals, cover -ups, poor standards of
governance, and the shallow leadership of John Key.
He now fronts up only if he looks good. Otherwise, it has to be the faceless Mr
Eagleson, the chief executive officer of the Prime Minister’s office, the guy who is the
fall guy for every mistake the Prime Minister makes. I have to wonder how this poor
man has ever kept his job , because he has been blamed for so many cock -ups that he
ought not to still be in the job. Whenever the Prime Minister fails to know about
something, we hear: “Oh, his CEO forgot to tell him. He did not tell him on time. He
waited 2 weeks. It slipped his mind.” Well, I think that the truth is going to come out. A
different version is going to come out in the future. I think that the truth will come out
when Mr Eagleson takes up his new job in the business sector. Then we will find out
how he became the fal l guy for a Prime Minister who would not front up to his own
foibles.
For years the National Party has banged on about a divided Labour Party. Well, I
have got bad news for the Government. We have got our act together. We are a united
team behind Andrew L ittle and some very talented members of Parliament who are
determined to take this Government on. But you know what I am observing? It happens
over time with a Government that has been around for a while and has got too cocky.
The instability starts to rise in its own party. Some of us have been around long enough.
We have seen it all —the instability in our party and the growing instability in its own
party. You only have to look at Judith Collins. Judith Collins was the fall guy for the
Prime Minister during the election campaign. You know what she is doing now? She is
talking to the ACT Party about joining it. She is talking to the ACT Party about joining
it because she knows she will never be the leader of the National Party. I have to say I
stopped for a  moment when I heard that. I was told by a very reliable source. I had to
stop for a minute, and I thought: “My God. Imagine the co-leadership of that party when
Judith is on board. You would have the captain and the cabin boy together.” That would
be the leadership of the ACT Party.
What we are seeing is a widening rift between Bill English and the Prime Minister.
Bill English is a hard -working, decent man with principles. I have always admired Bill
English because I know he lives his principles and he believes them. He now has to dea l
with a Prime Minister he once said bounces from cloud to cloud. But, unfortunately for
Bill English and his colleagues, John Key now bounces from cloud- cuckoo-land to
cloud-cuckoo-land. That is what is happening to the Prime Minister. You cannot believe
what he says any longer. Then we have Nick Smith. Government members put him up
to front their inadequacies in housing policy. They think if he talks long and loud
enough, we will not remember what the message was. Poor old Nick Smith—totally
isolated in his own party, scoffed at by his own colleagues.
Then we get to Steven Joyce, the most talked- about man—behind his back—in the
caucus. He is widely disliked for his arrogance and his bullying. You see, I actually
1554 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
quite like him, but then I do not have to share the Cabinet room with him. But members
opposite, with the widening rift between them, can see that this man wants the top job.
But others have got their eye on it. The woman who has just sat down, Paula Benne tt, is
so puffed up now because some bloggers wrote that she has taken over from Judith as
the next leader of the National Party. Well, of course she is eyeing Steven Joyce. They
are nudging each other out of the way, trying to find their place as the next  leader of the
National Party. What we have seen over these last 6 years is a passing parade of
Ministers who have left, who were incompetent, and who were involved in underhand
activities and cover -ups. Mr Deputy Speaker, I am very disappointed that you a re not
still in a ministerial role —a man of integrity and hard work. I cannot say the same for
those who have come and gone.
This Government does not have any solutions. What it has is just jibber -jabber. That
is what we will call it— the “Jibber -Jabber Go vernment”. We are going to see plenty
more of it. Every speech I have listened to in this debate has been nothing more than a
whole lot of slogans that do not address the issues facing us. Where are the real
solutions to the problem in Iraq? All we are doi ng is putting up our hands and saying:
“Wherever the US goes, we go.” Why not put down some real, concrete things we could
do to help the people in Iraq, those who need humanitarian aid, those who need medical
assistance, those who need refuge from that country? What do we get? “Yes, if America
invites us, we will go.” Well, let us be honest and open with the public of New Zealand.
Real policies and real debate—I am not expecting that from this Government.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.role: Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector
items.text: As I
rise and stand in the House and address it for the first time in this year, I am going to do
something that might cause alarm for those w ho are listening. I am going to tell a story
from our 1 -day caucus. I want to assure the members of this House that at our 1 -day
caucus about 10 days ago the mood of the members present was relaxed, refreshed,
excited, and ready to get on with the job of being in Government. Far be it from anyone
listening in the House this afternoon to believe the rhetoric that we have just heard from
the member opposite that there were any dull eyes at all, because that was so far from
the truth.
As the Government prepares itself for the year ahead —a year after an overwhelming
mandate on election day from the public of New Zealand, a year in which we will need
to get a lot of work done, which is the nature of the year after an election—we will
continue with the very four main priorities that we have set. They are the things that the
public of New Zealand tell us are important to them. The people of Rangitata tell me
that they want our economy to be stronger and more prosperous. They want the
Government to responsibly manage the money we take off them in taxes. They want us
to look at every single way we spend their taxpayer funding and make sure we are
getting the best bang for every single buck, because they could use it well themselves if
we left it in their pocket.
They want to know that we are using new ways to build a more competitive and
productive economy. They know that the signs are good because we have told them that
80,000 new jobs have been created in the last year. They know that the desire for
employment reflects the confidence the people of New Zealand have in getting a job.
They are seeking a job in ever -increasing numbers, so we have engagement in the
workforce that has never been seen before. That is a very good sign of confidence in
New Zealand. We are del ivering better public services, and we have so many examples
of that. We have examples where we have actually changed the goalposts because we
have achieved them sooner than we thought we would.
So far be it from there being any dull eyes on this side of the House —in fact, there is
an air of excitement. It is a tough job to get on and deliver to the public of New Zealand.
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1555
I want to go through some things. Members may have heard these before, but that is one
thing about this side of the House: we have all got the same message for the public of
New Zealand. We do not shy from that. If the public or the members of this House have
heard it all before—that is just because we agree with each other. We like each other.
And that is what makes this a strong National Government.
The last of our four priorities I want to touch on is rebuilding Christchurch —a tough
job. And still for many Christchurch residents there is a long way to go. But the
National Government is not shirking from that. Tonight the people of Chris tchurch will
celebrate, with up to 1 billion viewers around the world, the opening of the Cricket
World Cup. What an honour to have that happening on the Mainland in Christchurch.
After the House rises tonight, I hope to make my way to Christchurch and enj oy that
free event along with many other New Zealanders.
I want to touch now on our economic plan and the way that that is actually
influencing the lives of New Zealanders or Kiwis. The economy has grown by 3.2
percent in the year to September last year. That is one of the highest growth rates in the
developed world. We do see headlines in papers around the world that tell us that others
are envious of that and are asking how we are managing to achieve that. Average wages
have increased by 15 percent over the past 5 years and they are forecast to continue to
increase. Employment is growing. I have already touched on the 80,000 new jobs over
the last year, and 217,000 more people are employed than 5 years ago. It would be fair
to say we had a real low as a nation with the global financial crisis, the earthquakes, and
other disasters befalling the people of New Zealand, but there are 217,000 more jobs
than 5 years ago.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: Strong recovery.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: That is a str ong recovery. The cost of living increases are
very low right now. Inflation is at just 0.8 percent for the 2014 calendar year. That is
alongside the average weekly wage growth of 2.5 percent.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: So wages are growing faster than inflation.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: I know! It is funny —that does not seem to get discussed by
the Opposition. Unemployment still remains lower than most other countries, and we
seem to be heading in the right direction in terms of the growth in jobs. The balance of
payments deficit —well, the difference between what New Zealand earns and spends
around the world has narrowed to 2.6 percent of GDP. That is about a third of the deficit
of 6 years ago —on track again. We are on track and working towards a chieving a
Budget surplus this year.
Net Crown debt is going to fall to 20 percent of GDP by 2020, but we need to stick
to the plan. That plan is to make sure we are careful with the public purse, careful with
the money the taxpayers of New Zealand pay into the Crown accounts, and careful like
a previous Government would not know how to be, clearly, from the way we have had
to change things. Mortgage interest rates are now expected to stay lower for longer, and
more Kiwis than way, way back are flocking ba ck to New Zealand from Australia.
Certainly what we saw under the previous Government was a flood of New Zealanders
leaving. The seats of the whole of the Cake Tin would have been filled by the people
who were going to Australia. New Zealand is in good sha pe and getting to be in better
shape.
I want to touch now on an announcement that my colleague the Hon Nathan Guy
made today, because there are still challenges here in New Zealand. Yes, the milk
payout is quite low and that has challenged dairy farmers t o think about their budgets
and to think about their inputs. Then we have today the declaration of a medium -scale
adverse event due to the drought conditions on the East Coast of the South Island. Some
people will say we have declared drought. We have not. I live there, and the drought has
1556 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
been there for a while. In fact, if we were going to declare drought, we would have done
it last year. To some in the Opposition, apparently that is all you had to do to make it
rain. Some people say all you have to do is  have a cricket match locally and that will
make it rain.
The reality is that there has been already the rural support trust actively involved in
supporting the farmers in the Rangitata and in the whole of the area affected by the dry.
There has also alwa ys been the ability for people whose financial circumstances and
income change to go to Work and Income and to apply for grants if need be. There has
always been the ability for them to discuss with their accountant the change in
circumstances and to negot iate changes to their Inland Revenue taxation. So what we
have done now in declaring this is to give more money to the rural support trusts to
assist the people who require it and also so that the people who are in really straitened
circumstances have in t heir back pocket the ability to approach the Government for
more help. So it is really a bit psychological in terms of its support of farmers. They will
appreciate it. They do not have their hands out to the taxpayers of New Zealand saying
“Help us out.” w illy-nilly. We are having a rough year. It is a very hard thing for
farming families to ask for help —a very hard thing indeed—but the Minister for
Primary Industries has made the right call today.
I want to finish on an issue that is close to my heart. My  colleague the Hon Jonathan
Coleman is taking obesity very, very seriously. In my role as the Minister for Food
Safety I can say that we are doing our bit as well. Back in July last year New Zealand
adopted voluntary labelling by food companies with the Health Star Rating system. That
allows the public of New Zealand, when they see one of these Health Star Rating labels,
to identify the nutritional value of packaged foods.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: How many companies do it?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Eight companies have already—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Eight—eight! Oh, my goodness!

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: It may shock those opposite that Foodstuffs and Progressive
Enterprises are pretty big. The members opposite were com plaining about it not too
long ago. Those companies have said that 500 products of theirs will be on the shelf
with their new labels, having finished with their old labels, by the end of this year. So
members opposite may be very surprised to know that thi s is a good news story. This is
good news. This is actually this Government addressing obesity.

items.speaker: Iain Lees -Galloway
items.text: Do you get a manual? You need a manual just to read the
flaming label, you’ve made it so complicated.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: It is not complex at all, but it may be for the members
opposite. I am happy to give the members opposite a briefing about how simple it is if
they need some help. But the industry uptake has been excellent. This is something with
Australia and New Zealand working together, and it is an exciting way of addressing
obesity. Thank you.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to be
back in the House for 2015 and I have to say that it has never been more enjoyable to be
a member of the Labour caucus. Like my colleagues I went away and had a fantastic
summer. I enjoyed a lot of time with my family, I enjoyed a f ew barbecues, and, I can
tell you what, at those barbecues I heard one refrain over and over again: “Oh, I like that
Mr Little. We like that Mr Little.” That is what I was hearing all summer long from
people around my electorate and around the country, bec ause New Zealanders really
like Andrew Little. They see him as a straight shooter, a straight talker, and they
compare him with John Key —that slippery Mr Key, the man whom you just have to
look at and you know when he is not being completely honest. You know from his body
language, when he starts to shift a little bit from side to side, and from the old hissing
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1557
sound. We all know about that. New Zealanders instinctively know that John Key is
getting shiftier and shiftier and they now have a Leader of the Opposition who is an
absolute straight talker and who is taking it to John Key.

items.speaker: I will tell you what
items.text: it feels fantastic in the Labour caucus. I have gone away and I
am a little bit thinner, I am a little bit hairier, but I am ready to come back and take th e
fight to the National Government. I listened very closely to what the Prime Minister had
to say in his statement. I listened very closely and I wanted to hear particularly what he
had to say about employment relations, and it was not much. I was listening very
closely to hear whether this Government is prepared to take action on one of the most
insidious issues in employment relations right now —not just here in New Zealand but
in other countries like us—and that is the issue of zero-hour contracts.
Zero-hour contracts are something that we have seen proliferate in the wake of the
financial crisis and in the wake of the unmitigated attack on workers’ rights that we
have seen year after year from this National Government. There are now thousands of
New Zeal anders who are stuck on these zero- hour contracts. What is a zero- hour
contract? It is a contract where the worker has to make themselves available for work at
all times, but there is no requirement whatsoever on the employer to provide that worker
with work. They are, therefore, very different from casual contracts. Casual contracts
can provide flexibility both for the employer and the employee, but it is an absolutely
one-sided relationship with these zero- hour contracts, and we see more and more of
them every day, particularly in the fast -food industry but also increasingly in
supermarkets and in the retail industry. We know that we are just going to see more and
more of them if the Government does not take action.
So that is what I was listening for in the Prime Minister’s speech —what was he
going to do about zero -hour contracts? The answer was nothing. There was not a
mention of it —not one. So today I lodged my Employment Relations (Certainty at
Work) Amendment Bill, which takes aim at zero -hour contracts and seeks to rule them
out from our employment relations framework. So what will have to happen is that
employers will have to give an indication of how many hours a worker can expect to get
if they have to be available for work at all times. It still a llows flexibility—of course,
we have to strike a balance between flexibility and certainty at work —but it gives
workers an idea of how much work they can expect to get from one week to the next, so
that they can plan, so that they can put food on the table  for their children every single
week, so that they can go to the bank and talk about getting a loan or a mortgage, and so
that they can do things that we used to take for granted. We used to believe that if you
got a job, you would be able to make ends meet, provide for your family, and get ahead.
But these zero -hour contracts make life utterly insecure for ordinary working people,
and we are seeing them used more and more every day. This Government has
completely ignored that issue.
On this side of the House we are prepared to take action. We are prepared to do what
is required to ensure that our Employment Relations Act ceases the use of these zero -
hour contracts and gives workers certainty whilst also ensuring that employers have
flexibility. Brett Patterson works for Burger King in Hamilton. He is one of thousands
of employees who are in the fast -food industry on zero- hour contracts. He says it is
incredibly hard to make a living. He says he always finds himself having to fight to get
the hours he needs . He says it is even worse when you are sick because if you are sick,
you cannot be there to fight for the hours that you need to make ends meet. How many
hours a worker on a zero -hour contract gets can be everything from zero to 20, to 40, to
5, to 60 hours, and it often depends on how good a relationship you have with the
person who does the rosters. If you have a falling -out with the person who does the
1558 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
rosters, you can quickly find yourself getting fewer and fewer hours, maybe even not
being asked to come to work at all. That is the reality for ordinary working people.
So I looked for a response from John Key. I looked to see what the Prime Minister
thought about this issue that affects so many ordinary New Zealanders, and I found one.
I was surprised, but I found one. The Prime Minister’s answer to workers on zero- hour
contracts: get advice. Go and get some legal advice before you sign up to one of these
things. Well, that sounds all fine and dandy but it just shows you how utterly out of
touch with reality John Key is. If a worker turns down a zero- hour contract at Burger
King, Wendy’s, McDonalds, Glassons, or Hallensteins, then there will 10, 20, or 30
other people lining up to take that job instead of them.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: These things are nothing new. What’s new about this, Mr Lees -
Galloway?

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: That is the reality —that is the reality. Brett Hudson
asks what is new about it. What is new about it is that unemployment has gone up under
this National Government so far more people are competing for jobs than ever had to
compete for jobs before. So every time a worker goes along and is offered a zero- hour
contract, if they take advice or if they try to bargain with the employer, then it is down
the road, my friend; there is the door. The employer will take one of the 50 othe r people
who applied for that job.
So John Key is absolutely out of touch on this issue, and he has broken so many
promises to workers. I remember that when National came to office its big goal for
workers was to close the wage gap with Australia. When National came to office the
average wage gap with Australia was $121.76 a week; today it is $170.28 a week.
National has demonstrably failed on one of the key tasks it set itself, and it has broken a
promise to ordinary workers. I hear the National members t alking about how average
wages are going up in New Zealand. Well, whoop- de-doo! We know how the average
wage is going up in New Zealand. It is the rich getting richer. The people on high
incomes, on high wages, are seeing their wages going up, and everybod y else is being
left behind. That is how average wages go up in this country.
Take a look at median incomes. If you are serious about getting things sorted for
ordinary working people, take a look at median incomes and you will see that in real
terms they have fallen year on year—

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: Wages are rising faster than inflation.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: —under this National Government. Average wages are
rising, Mr Hudson. I know you cannot get your head around this. I know it is a bit of a
complicated thing that you have to understand. Average wages may be rising, but that is
a result of people on high wages getting richer —the National Party’s mates getting
richer—and everybody else being left behind.
On this side of the House we know that it takes more than productivity gains, it takes
more than a strong economy. Those things are important, but we need to make sure that
we have our legislation right, that we have our regulations right, and that we enforce
minimum standards so that workers can get a fair share of a growing economy. Right
now workers are not getting a fair share, and that is National’s legacy.

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: It is really an honour to
speak in the debate on the Prime Minister’s statement today. It is somewhat confusing
because if you were to listen to the speeches of the Opposition members, you would
think that New Zealanders up and dow n this country are in a mood of doom and gloom
and there is nothing positive on our horizon. I can say only that if you reflect on the
mood at Waitangi this year, there was a bit of hype and conversation about how
combative it might be. But I actually thin k Waitangi Day is a really good illustration of
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1559
the mood of the nation. It was quiet. It was peaceful. There were not protests. There was
not frustration.
It is really interesting because the speaker before me, Iain Lees -Galloway, talked
about the fact th at the leader of the country should be in touch with ordinary New
Zealanders. There is no way that the National Party would have got close to 50 percent
of the support of all New Zealanders in the election last year if we had a leader who was
not in touch with ordinary hard- working New Zealanders. Of course, what are they
interested in? They are interested in having more jobs available. They are interested in
their wages going up. They are interested in interest rates remaining low. They are
interested in u nemployment rates falling. That is exactly the results that the first two
terms of the National Government led by Prime Minister John Key have delivered, and
we are keeping our promises to hard- working New Zealanders. We are focusing on the
issues that matter to them: raising education standards, lowering crime, providing better
access to health services, and genuinely and generally improving the lives of ordinary
New Zealanders and their families.
I think it is quite the opposite of Annette King’s suggest ion that this side of the
House is not energised and excited. I can tell you this Government is raring to go,
enthusiastic, and energetic about what we have in front of us, which is quite different
from the mood, if you were watching, when Andrew Little de livered his first speech in
the House this year. It felt awkward and awful, and the Opposition benches were trying
to be enthused about the kick-off of their leader this year.
I want to focus on a couple of specific areas. The previous speaker, Iain Lees -
Galloway, talked about the employment market. He talked about the workforce in quite
a lot of detail. What he did not say is that in terms of the latest household labour force
survey, women’s participation in the labour market and women’s employment are at
record highs. He did not mention that. He was not excited about that. It must have been
a bit disturbing for his female caucus members who I would have thought should have
been quite excited about those sorts of statistics. I know I am. The participation rate for
women is 64.6 percent and the employment rate is 60.4 percent. They are the highest
since the survey began in 1986. So that is what this Government is delivering: great
news for women up and down New Zealand. I want to cut into it in more detail: 7,300
more Māori women and 1,800 more Pasifika women are in employment than in
December 2013. Again, they are results we should be celebrating and I am not hearing
the celebrations from the other side of the House.
We are relevant. This side of the House focuses on the issues that matter to New
Zealanders. Prime Minister John Key in his very first speech said he would lead a
Government for all New Zealanders and that is exactly what he is doing. If you look at
where some of this growth in women’s employment is occurring, Canterbury is a great
example. Women are playing a really critical part in the rebuilding of Canterbury. An
example is that there are 7,700 more women employed in Canterbury than at the same
time in 2013. Part of that is because of the cons ideration of girls and women looking at
what were considered non- traditional employment opportunities. That is where the
growth is. So as Minister for Women I have committed to having some courageous
conversations with business, with community, and with families about what some of the
biases are that exist for girls and women that restrict their opportunities and their
opportunities for economic independence in New Zealand.
One aspect of this is the current gender pay gap. You know, I have had a number of
people who have asked me why we even have a Minister for Women. Well, it is
incredibly clear to me that while we have a gender pay gap of 9.9 percent, there is work
for the Ministry for Women. But it is not just women in the workforce that I want to
focus on, because if you look at other areas that are critical to them, some of them are
1560 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
very clearly around their families. When we talk about employment relations
legislation—the speaker before me did not say anything about the Act that we have just
passed. He  did not say anything about the fact that part of that legislation was for
flexible workplaces and flexible work practices. So no longer is it just the fact that
somebody has caregiving responsibilities that means they can ask their employer for
flexible w ork arrangements. I think that in terms of women in the workforce it is an
incredible advantage, and I have been waiting to hear the Opposition members who
pride themselves on being the champions for the workers to celebrate this incredible
result for wome n in our workplaces. But no, they tend to be fairly silent on that one.
This is a Government that recognises the diverse and very different needs of workers.
This is a Government that is delivering for workers and that is just one example.

items.speaker: I want to give you another example
items.text: paid parental leave. This is a Government that is
focusing on making sure that our paid parental leave and our parental tax credits are
actually accessible and available to more New Zealand families, and that is something I
am incredibly proud of, because when we have families where women or men choose to
be in the workplace, we want to provide the opportunities and provide the support that
they need to get ahead.
One of the clear areas that I as the Minister for Women will continue to  focus on is
reducing violence. We have already made some good inroads in terms of reducing crime
rates in this country and reducing reoffending. But I am very clear that our homes and
our communities should be the safest places for New Zealanders and particularly for our
young girls and our women. That is why, working with my ministerial colleagues on
this area of domestic violence, we will be finding more ways and broader ways of
reaching out and working with others to ensure that that level of violence i s decreasing
and looking at unique solutions that actually work for families and work in
communities.
The other clear area that I am responsible for is the area of land information, and this
is an area where not many people are actually aware of the contr ibution that this makes
to our economy. We have a system of property rights in New Zealand that is very robust
and very strong and that really underpins a lot of information and a lot of decisions that
we make in central government and also across business es. Just recently the 2014- 15
Open Data Barometer global report showed that New Zealand continues to be one of the
best countries in the world at allowing open access to Government data —and of course
open data is a key indicator of a country’s innovation, transparency, and lack of
corruption. If you were fortunate to attend the New Zealand Spatial Excellence Awards
like I did last year, you would realise the wizardry of some of our New Zealanders in
terms of using location information to solve some of the very large challenges that we
face as a country and it is underpinning an important part of our economic recovery.
In closing, I want to say that we really are living in exciting times. We have a
country that is growing and expanding, and where we are reducing things like crime and
raising educational achievement. This is a Government that is raring to go. This is not a
Government that is anywhere near having completed our work and our plan. We are in
this together and we are, fortunately, led by a Prime Mi nister who has said very clearly
that we are not here to fill the green seats; we are here to do a lot for New Zealand. We
have done a lot, there is still a lot more to go, and it is great to know that nearly one in
every two New Zealanders is backing us. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: The speaker who has just sat down,
Louise Upston, did not address the issue that many New Zealanders are thinking about
at the moment, and that i s sending our troops and our forces into harm’s way, into Iraq.
If you look at what has happened over the last months, the months of being able to
respond to this, it is an utter muddle. What we know is that the Government has already
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1561
taken a decision on t his issue and is arrogantly allowing New Zealanders to think that
somehow it is still considering its options. Training has been going on for months, and
this week Gerry Brownlee rather arrogantly said that somehow there was going to be
some preliminary tr aining for a possible deployment in Iraq. His office told us that in
December last year. Last year we knew what the training was for, and this week we get
told by Gerry Brownlee that, actually, he has made a decision around that.
The Government cannot continue to fool the country on an issue as serious as that.
But to beat that were Murray McCully’s comments today on radio and what he was
actually saying about our deploying into Iraq. There have been no Government -to-
Government discussions about deployment in Iraq up until now. We have been training
for 3 months but there has been no discussion with the Iraqis about putting our troops
on their soil, helping them out, or even asking them whether they actually want New
Zealand forces to be there. In fact, he went on to say to journalists that that has actually
been done by the US and Australia on our behalf. This is really about what John Key
admitted to a BBC interviewer —it is about being part of the club. This is not about
making a real difference. It is being part of that club, a club of the willing that wants to
go in there. Of course, the US and Australia, who are already there, want us to be part of
their club—and the UK. The Foreign Secretary of the UK was here last week, and he
too wanted New Zealand to be part of that club. When I asked the UK Foreign Secretary
how many troops the UK has on the ground and how many troops it is planning to
deploy, the answer was none —zero. The British Government does not want to put
troops on the  ground, because it believes it is politically untenable in Britain. Why?
Because it realises, after 10 years of putting troops on the ground there, that people in
Britain do not want to go down the same route again.
When you look at the legacy, the history, of Western involvement in the Middle East,
it turns out to be not a pretty history. Yet we are making a decision on behalf of New
Zealanders. We have already made it—it has been done. It has all been wrapped up. We
have had our meetings with our partic ular club, and we will be putting in troops on the
ground as a result of that. What has changed, because John Key realises that the club
conversation is not working, is that for the first time I have heard John Key address
human rights. Suddenly, human rig hts are being pulled out of the drawer and human
rights are being used as the justification of why we need to be in Iraq. Well, human
rights violations are occurring right across the world—certainly in Iraq; what has been
done by the Islamic State is barbaric and horrible. But they are also happening with
Boko Haram and, oddly enough, they are also happening in Sri Lanka, a country, we
