learnt this week, whose former president, Mr Rajapaksa, has been invited by John Key
to come to New Zealand on a formal vis it. This is a man who presided over 50,000
Tamils being killed and has not done any investigation into that issue, and yet John Key,
standing up for human rights in one situation, is conveniently ignoring human rights in
another.
What New Zealanders want when the Government is thinking about going into a war
zone and a conflict zone —and do not believe that we will be operating behind the wire
and therefore everything will be OK and will be risk- free. That is not the case, and it is
not the situation that h as been experienced by any trainer in the Middle East or
Afghanistan. Many casualties have occurred behind the so- called wire, whatever that
wire might be. What we expect, what New Zealand expects, and what the Labour Party
expects—and a Labour Government has committed troops into conflicts before —is a
sound analysis and a sound rationale for why we want to be there. I do not believe that
this Government has answered the hard questions we expect to be answered. What is
going to happen is that 2 years down t he track we are going to be asking why we are
there and what the purpose is.
1562 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
Here are some of the questions. Can we make a difference? Surely that is a question
that we have to ask ourselves —can we make a difference? The United States spent $25
billion over 10 years, at the cost of scores if not hundreds of its soldiers, training the
Iraqi Army only to find that it did not succeed and that the army did not stand up the
first time it went into battle. Much of that problem was not to do with the training.
Much of that problem was to do with fact that the political environment had undermined
and hollowed out that military. But that is what I mean. What can we do—putting a
band-aid over something like that —that will make a real difference to the Iraqis and to
the Iraqi armed forces. What is the risk? What is the assessment of that risk to New
Zealand? I do not believe that we have done that. We are gung -ho about going in. The
Australians went in without being asked, actually. They positioned their forces outside
of Iraq without being asked, then tried to ask their way in. Of course, they want us to be
there. They want another flag up the pole. The question is what the risk is to our
soldiers, and I do not believe that has been answered. What is the exit strategy?  How do
we know when this mission is complete? We sent troops into Bamian with a very clear
set of instructions. This Government eventually pulled them out, after believing that
what we had done and the mission that we had set out to achieve had been compl eted as
far as it could. That is not the case in this situation. The US is asking for just a 3- year
commitment to put more troops on the ground. That looks to me like a slippery slope
that we are embarking on without an exit strategy.
What is the risk to ordinary New Zealanders, to Kiwis right across this country, of
Islamic State and the radicalisation that is happening by becoming engaged in a conflict
like Iraq? That has not been assessed. That has certainly not been assessed. What is the
risk to New Ze alanders here and abroad from our being more involved in this conflict,
and what is the cost? Another question: what is the cost of that involvement by putting
100-odd New Zealand troops on the ground? And how could we better use that money?
What are the opportunity costs? What are the opportunities in humanitarian assistance—
in standing beside some of the organisations and the local authorities and Governments
that are desperately trying to address the real underlying issues that are causing the
conflict in Iraq to start with? The economic issues, the capacity issues within the
Government that have allowed that military to fall apart—those are issues where we can
actually really make a difference, I believe, and we have not been able to address those
at all.
Lastly, here at home, what are we doing to address the possible radicalisation of
young Muslims, in particular, on the ground? Everybody whom I have met has told me
that that simply is not happening. Yet when we look at risks to New Zealand, those are
the risks that we need to address, which we are simply not doing. Instead, we are going
and embarking on a military adventure to join a club.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. Ian
McKelvie—5 minutes.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I am fortunate to have the opportunity to
be a National Party member of Parliament, representing the Rangitīkei electorate, in a
unique time in New Zealand’s history. My electorate has been part of this House for the
entire 153 years of its existence, and I do not think that ever in that time has this country
been led by a more talented team of Ministers and, in turn, a great Prime Minister.
Never in that time have we been more respected in the world of politics, with a seat on
the UN Security Council to boot. Never in that time has our economy performed as well
as it is doing now, at a time of comparative difficulty in the rest of the Western World.
Never have we had such an opportunity to capitalise on the hard work of our forefathers
and mothers in setting up a country with such magnificent potential. And on the
doorstep we have the biggest market we have probably ever seen in our lifetime. It is a
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1563
far cry from 150 years ago, this weekend, when the first shipment of lambs set off for
the old mother country —for some of you, England; not for me, I might add. It is, of
course, the year of the sheep in China and that bodes w ell for our sheep industry in this
country, as you can tell.
Last September, after what can only be described as a testing election campaign, this
John Key -  led Government was returned to the Treasury benches with the largest
public vote in history. It was a just reward for some very hard work and great support
from so many New Zealanders who knew they were doing better than they could
possibly do under the alternatives on offer.
I wish to pick up on a couple of themes from the Prime Minister’s statement. The
first, and the most critical to our futures, is the proposal to amend the Resource
Management Act to help ease costs on businesses wishing to grow the New Zealand pie.
I am confident this can be achieved without threat to our environment. You see, that
confidence is well placed. As this Government knows, the tourism and agriculture
sectors rely heavily on our pristine environment to grow and prosper in the future.
Agriculture makes a massive contribution to our economy and right now is being tested
a little by the dry.
I want to make the point that farms are bu sinesses. This is summer and we, like any
other businesses, protect ourselves and understand our risks. We make allowance for
storms, droughts, and even disease. However, like all other sectors, some will always
need a hand in adversity. The Minister for P rimary Industries well recognises that fact
and has acted today in South Canterbury and North Otago. The real downside of
drought, of course, is the drop in production, and that affects the income this country
gets. It cuts the amount of money going around in the economy. It cuts the amount of
revenue the Government collects, and consequently the amount we can spend on our
programmes, on achieving the things we want to achieve as a Government.
Many of those other things we want to achieve are very relevant  to the Rangitīkei,
and include the following. I want to talk briefly about freshwater reform. This will
continue through the recommendations of the Land and Water Forum as will the
investment in regional water infrastructure and storage. Water storage is a very exciting
opportunity for this country, as it creates the opportunity, when managed and planned
properly, to assist our rivers, help our environmental challenge, and generate income —
both recreational and agricultural. It is one of the most important things we can
concentrate on as a country.
Workplace safety is crucial to the Rangitīkei electorate. Forestry and agriculture both
have some significant issues to deal with here, which we must pay close attention to,
and our sectors must work closely with WorkSafe New Zealand to make some very
quick improvements in this area. The Rural Broadband Initiative has made good
progress under this Government and will continue through the initiative to improve
mobile coverage and broadband connectivity in rural and  remote areas. Another very
important factor for our rural areas is that it builds our population potential. The
Government’s new housing initiative fits beautifully into my electorate. An outstanding
example of how well it works exists in the Manawatū Com munity Trust, set up by the
Manawatū District Council to own its 208 community houses. Those residents now
have an entity that cares for them, and warm, comfortable, appropriately sized houses,
and I very much hope they will get the opportunity to participate in this latest offering.
The people of my electorate significantly benefit from Whānau Ora, one of the
legacies of the Hon Dame Tariana Turia and one I am very pleased about continuing to
support. The Treaty process is also having a very positive effec t on rural New Zealand,
and we look forward to the completion of that process. My electorate contains the bulk
of the New Zealand defence forces, at Linton, Ōhākea, and  Waiōuru, and our decisions
1564 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
in respect of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant will have an effect here, as will the
activities as we continue to celebrate World War I. There is so much being undertaken
by this very busy Government, but I must leave it here. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Jami-Lee Ross—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: It is very good to be back in the House
after the summer adjournment. It is good to be back with my caucus colleagues, who are
right behind our leader, the Prime Minister of New Zealand, a Prime Minister who is
achieving good things for New Zealanders and is seeing a country that is much better
off than it was 6 years ago after 9 years of a dreadful period of G overnment led by the
Labour Party.
If anyone was listening to the debate this afternoon on the Prime Minister’s
statement, they could be led to believe that Labour was sitting there just before an
election, ready to take over, rejuvenated and united behind its leader. Those of us who
have been watching politics for more than just the last hour realise that that is not the
case at all. We heard Annette King talking about a tired Government that needed to
rejuvenate and was a bit arrogant, in her view. The t hing about Annette King is that she
has seen that many times before— and not just at the end of the 2008 period of the
Labour Government. She also saw that back in the 1980s when the Labour Party, during
her first time around, was at exactly the same point.  Annette King likes to talk about a
tired Government because she has been part of so many tired Governments. So I think
she is talking about her own team when she talks about a tired set of members of
Parliament.
Then we heard from Mr Lees -Galloway. Mr Le es-Galloway was telling us that
Labour has been having another barbecue season. He was quite open about it, very open
about it—another barbecue season. The interesting thing about the barbecue season he
spoke about was that he talked to only four people at  the barbecue. The four people he
talked to at the barbecue were the four people who think Andrew Little is a good leader
of the Labour Party. We know —we know for a fact —that Andrew Little has only four
members of his party in his caucus supporting him. Tony Abbott is actually more
popular than that in his party at the moment. Andrew Little is struggling for support. Mr
Lees-Galloway was also sporting a beard. The last person who went away over summer
and came back with a beard was David Cunliffe. I know that Mr Lees -Galloway was a
sycophant of David Cunliffe, so maybe there is another leadership coup coming round
the corner.
Then we heard David Shearer, the man who came from the UN with strong human
rights credentials, standing up in the House and arguing about John Key’s desire to see
New Zealand potentially help those who are facing human rights grievances around the
world. David Shearer has now abandoned his human rights credentials. He no longer
believes that New Zealand has a part to play. I actually u sed to have a lot of respect for
David Shearer, and I am starting to question whether that respect was properly founded.
I am part of the National Party because I believe we need to grow wages in this
country and we need to get more people into jobs in this country. I believe that more
children need access to education, and I believe that more children and older people
should get access to the operations and the health services they need. We also need to
see more people getting access to housing in this co untry. Those are the things that this
Government is delivering for New Zealanders.
I found it very interesting that the Labour leader liked to talk in his state of the nation
speech, just after the summer period, about jobs and wages —something that Labour has
apparently woken up to. The interesting thing about that is that National is de livering
more jobs for New Zealanders. National is delivering higher wages for New Zealanders.
In the last year, 80,000 New Zealanders got into work. They came off the dole queue,
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1565
came out of unemployment, came out of training, and got jobs —80,000 more people.
Average wages are also up and going faster than inflation. New Zealanders are
wealthier. More New Zealanders are in jobs.
We are delivering on exactly the things that Andrew Little thinks Governments
should be delivering on. In fact, I saw his speech as a bit of a vote of confidence, apart
from the fact that he has created a job for Mr Grant Robertson to go around and set up a
commission because he is looking a bit bored at the moment. You have got to give your
leadership opponents an opportunity to do something else, and that is what is happening
with Mr Robertson. But we are delivering. We are doing what New Zealanders want.
We have the support of New Zealanders. When Labour talks about the National Party
looking after its mates, the thing about it is that we have got so many mates around the
country. We are looking after them. We are looking after all New Zealanders. That is
why I am proud to be on this side of the House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. Jo
Hayes—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. As this is my first call for the
year, I want to wish you a happy New Year. To all the members of the House and
parliamentary staff, a happy New Year to you too. I am so pleased to be back in the
House. It beats running around after 1,500 ewes, trying to move them with a dog that
will not listen.
As I stand and reflect on the years since National became Government, I am
reminded of the challenges that this Government faced when first taking office in 2008.
I am astounded— yes, astounded—that the members opposite me can stand and take a
crack at this Government over the way we have managed t he financial situation of this
country to date. What a cheek —what a cheek. In 2008—and I have said this in past
speeches, because the memories of the left seem to be a little bit wanting—

items.speaker: Hon Louise Upston
items.text: More than a little.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Yes, more than that. Yes, in 2008 this Government found the
country’s coffers were bare. The breeze was blowing through from one side of the safe
to the other, and the country was in deficit, a deficit that should not have been there,
especially when the left had been boasting of surpluses. Surpluses, my foot —no
evidence; it did not happen. We all know now, so you are caught out, the left. To
members on the left, I say: stop harping on about all the good old days. I can tell you
now—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: The good old days when we were in Government.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: —it was an untruth, Megan. It was an untruth. You fooled the
country. Then, of course, while I am on a roll here, what about the Labour leadership? A
lot like the meteor last night: it builds up, gathers rubbish, burns out, and fizzles out.
So from bare coffers and a growing deficit this National -led Government took over.
We took over just when the global financial crisis hit and there was the collapse o f
financial companies. We came with a plan, and we were determined that we were going
to be pushing it through. Then came our two major tragedies —the Christchurch
earthquakes and the Pike River mine disaster. We needed support, and we got it. Yes,
we got that support because we have the right plan with the right people, and, of course,
the right leader. This is a stable and proven Government that delivers on what we say.
You will hear that many times from this side of the House, because we do deliver on
what we say. Essentially we are, and will continue to be, a can -do National -led
Government, and everybody knows it, in partnership with the Māori Party, United
Future, and ACT. We are here for all New Zealanders.
As I turn to the year ahead, one of the Gover nment’s key policies is housing. How
fortuitous is that? During the 2014 campaign I, along with other candidates in the
1566 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
Christchurch East electorate, was interviewed on a meet the candidates -  style CTV
programme. We were asked: “What keeps you up at night ?”. My response was
housing—housing in an electorate where a number of people and families either lost
their homes or required repairs.
During that time this Government opened its first social housing project in Aranui.
With the sod turned and the first homes built and occupied, the plan is to ensure more
homes will be available through our social housing policy, which has been launched and
is well under way. Just the other week I was taken on tour of a Housing New Zealand
social housing project in Christc hurch East. I am happy to report that I am looking
forward to seeing a number of housing projects completed before the year is out,
especially in Aranui.
I cannot extol enough the virtues of this Government’s policies when it comes to
housing and the rebuild of Christchurch, especially Christchurch East. From increased
housing comes employment; from employment comes growth; and from growth comes
wealth—wealth that benefits everyone as the economy continues to grow. This
National-led Government has a well-crafted financial plan, with its sights set on making
everything right in God’s own. This is something that I am sure the members on the left
have no idea of, or where to start. Really, it is “TL, TL, GBL” —too little, too late, and
goodbye to the left. Kia ora.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Todd Barclay—5 minutes.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: I want to  start by welcoming
everybody back after the New Year break and say what a pleasure it is to be part of a
united, excited, strong National caucus that supports our leader and our deputy leader. It
is a shame that the same cannot be said for the other side of the House, and it is a shame
that those members cannot unite themselves in the same way that we have.
Today I want to focus a little bit on education and the importance of a good
education in giving kids the best start in life. I particularly want to remind New
Zealanders of the mess that the previous Labour Government left the portfolio in when
we inherited it 6 years ago. Since we have entered Government we have increased
spending on education by 45 percent. We now spend more on education than on the
Ministry of Social Development and the Police combined. Unlike the previous Labour
Government we are looking at having all components of the education system in the
pipeline.
Since we have entered into Government we have more than doubled spending on
early childhood education. That equals what we spend on the Police budget. When we
took over, 93.6 percent of school starters had participated in early childhood education.
We have increased that to 96.1 percent, and we have got a target of 98 percent. That is
six and a half thousand more kids entering early childhood education before they start
school. In the primary sector we have set targets through the introduction of national
standards. We want 85 percent of kids achieving a level of reading, writing, and maths
before they exit out into the secondary sector. Currently, we are at 77.9 percent for
reading, 70.6 percent for writing, and 74.6 percent for maths.
Moving on to the secondary sector, we have made great gains in the National
Certificate of Education al Achievement (NCEA). Sure, Labour may have introduced
NCEA, but after Labour introduced it, it did nothing with it. There was a 68 percent
achievement rate in NCEA level 2 when we took over. We have increased that to 79
percent. We have got a target of 85 percent, so we are well on track. Moving on to level
4—post-school qualifications —when we came into Government, there were 53.3
percent of 25 to 35- year-olds who held New Zealand Qualifications Framework level 4
or equivalent. We have increased that to 54.7 percent, and we have almost met our
target of 55 percent 1 year early.
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1567
Since we came into Government we have been focused on implementing a seamless
transition throughout each sector of the education pipeline. That leads on to the
investment approach that we are taking in the social sector more generally. I want to use
two examples that Bill English cited during the campaign last year. The first is in
relation to teen sole parents on benefits. We have 2,600 of these people in our country.
They are all classified as being under the age of 20. If you are in this category, the
average expected time that you will spend on a benefit is 20 years, with a present net
cost to the taxpayer of $250,000 per person. Instead, we are choosing to spend $7,000 a
year on each of these people through implementing a supervising adult into their lives
and making sure that these people are getting re- engaged into education, learning a
tolerance level around budgeting, and being provided with other services that well equip
them for living in modern society. If we achieve that and if they achieve a post -school
qualification, the average expected time they will spend on a benefit reduces from 20
years down to 7 years. That saves the taxpayer millions of dollars.
The second group is the group of 2,000 kids who are currently in the toughest client
group, if you like, of the Government going forward. There was an analysis done of 30
years of their previous family records, based on their parents’ interaction with the
Government and t heir current interaction with the Government. We have valued the
projected expenditure on them over their lifetime, through prison costs alone, at $750
million. What we are deciding to do instead is re -engage them back in education and
ensure they complete their education and then enter the workforce with the ability to get
a job and not have to go on to a benefit. This is so that they do not fall into the justice
trap and offend and enter the justice system. These sole parents on benefits and the
toughest clients who are male children who are currently in the school sector—if we can
re-engage them, get them back on track through education, we will be doing them and
New Zealand a great service. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The Prime Minister’s statement on Tuesday
was steady as she goes. Setting aside the ribald and irrelevant commentary that peppers
his deliveries to the House these days, Mr Key strove to provide the usual reassurances
to the New Zealand people: sound fiscal management, support for business
entrepreneurship, State sector reform, and earthquake recovery. We have been on the
receiving end of this for 5 years now. It has become a mantra; a form of hypnopaedia —
a National lullaby for those who wish to be reassured, to retire to bed secure in the
knowledge that our nation is in good hands.
There was no penetrating and insightful comment on the global situation. Let us
consider what the Prime Minister had to say about the world out there. First, our tenure
on the Security Council places us, he observed, “at the heart of international decision
making.” New Zealand is determined, he said, to “effect real change” on the council.
“We have,” he said, “already demonstrated our willingn ess to be a strong independent
voice”. This comes a week after he advised the BBC, and thus the world, that
contributing military training to Iraq is the price of the club. “Ultimately,” he told the
world, “are we going to say we are going to be part of a club like [we] are with the Five
Eyes intelligence? Are we ultimately going to be able to rely on members of those clubs
to support us in our moment of need?”. Unless there be any uncertainly as to the nature
of the club, the Prime Minister, drawing himself up to the full height of responsible
global citizenship, added: “And we do know that, when it comes to the United States
and Canada and Australia and Great Britain and others, that we can rely on them.” And
what can we contribute? Well, not much, but a bit. He said: “Even if the contribution is
small—of course it will be proportional —there has to be some contribution. It is the
price of the club.”
1568 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
The Prime Minister merged his BBC interview in London with a side trip to Davos,
where his favourite club of clubs —the global business elite—tolerated his presence. He
was accompanied there by his “Minister for Trade and Dangerous Climate Change”,
Tim Groser, who said in the House last year that New Zealand was now being accepted
in “the big boys’ club” through his personal participation in the G20 and the World
Economic Forum. This kind of diplomacy titillates our national leader, fresh from
Christchurch a spiration and London currency markets, where club membership is
indeed the passport to financial and political power. As a result, 6 years into the John
Key Government the nation’s foreign policy is characterised by a certain “clubbiness”.
Congratulations and prizes to the nation’s two top club members.
There is a self -evident contradiction—a logical mistake —being made here. We
cannot say there has to be a contribution as the price of the club and then say we are
independent. Not even my 10 -year-old granddaughter would buy that line, nor her 8-
year-old sister. They were not born yesterday. I am not sure about their 3- year-old
cousin, but I would not want to subject the Prime Minister to his wrath, so I would
advise him to think carefully before double -speaking to the sons and daughters of this
country. The price of the club is the price of the club. That price is providing troops to
war-torn and weary places in response to pressure from the leaders of the club, even
when we are privately in doubt —even when w e say they are there for training. This is
how the Americans kicked off in Viet Nam 50 years ago. And if we are frantically
shoring up Iraq’s army today, has any club member asked the grand leader why it saw
such wisdom and vision 12 years ago in dismantling it?
I say to the Prime Minister that if you are an independent nation, you are not
beholden to a club—never. You abide by binding decisions of the United Nations. That
is being part of the human family. The so- called club, whose membership you value so
highly and hold in such personal esteem, illegally invaded the very country you are
sending our troops to again. The US, the UK, and Australia illegally invaded Iraq in
2003. Some club! What to call it —the lawbreakers? And we did it ourselves once,
before that. Back in 1956 we were torn between two members of our club: Britain and
Australia on the one hand, and the leading club member, the United States, on the other.
We sided with our closer cousins and invaded Egypt —also illegally. We got
censured and condemned by the Security Council on behalf of the larger human family.
We had to withdraw. It was a humiliating moment for the UK especially, signifying the
end of its global leadership. So we have a bit of a track record in sloping along inside
the club i nto military misadventure. At least we had the wisdom back in 2003 not to
follow the club into Iraq. There had not been an authorising Security Council resolution.
A majority on the council, including three permanent members, opposed military
intervention. Did this influence the leading club -ites? Not on your life —in they went.
But today the club is fractured. Britain is not sending troops; just bombing from a
height.
Where is the authorising resolution for this military action in Iraq in 2015? Is it
Resolution 2170? One permanent member says that that is not a basis for military
action. Is it collective self -defence under article 51? A bit of a long shot. We are a
member of the council now. We cannot do our usual thing and duck for cover. As a new
member, we are obliged to respect the council’s integrity. The Security Council is the
ultimate club when it comes to this sort of thing, not “Five Eyes”. Which club means
the most to us—the “Five Eyes” espionage network or the 15-member Security Council,
whose primary job it is to ensure international peace and security? Let us get our club
memberships sorted in order of priority, having regard to the standards of global
legitimacy.
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1569
About 1,000 years ago, our first settlers arrived here. They were not members of
John Key’s club. Almost two centuries ago, our European forebears came here to leave
the Victorian club back in the motherland. We are no longer members of the Anglo-
Saxon club that illegally invaded Egypt 50 years ago. We are no longer members of the
Pacific ANZUS club that got mired in Viet Nam, raining napalm down on villages. We
were never members of the trilateral club that invaded Iraq illegally 12 years ago. We
are, in fact, or need to be, an independent nation—considering the idea of a new flag to
prove the point—that is never beholden to a club.
If we are truly concerned by the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) —and we
should be—then we might ask ourselves a few club questions of a broader kind. Are
there any member States of the United Nations funding ISIL? If so, do they include
Saudi Arabia and Qatar? If so, what might be the club’s response? What about the
Security Council’s resolutions and its sanctions committees imposing obligations and
penalties on member States financing terror gro ups? Why is the legal integrity of the
intervention in Iraq not made clear by the UN Secretary-General, based on the advice of
his chief legal officer? Why does this Prime Minister not get a written opinion from his
Attorney-General on the legality of any decision involving New Zealand troops in Iraq
and table it in this Parliament so that the question can be debated?
This is the time to remind people of the horrors of war and to outline a better path.
Are our sons and daughters going into armed conflict s o that this Prime Minister can be
part of a club of some dubious legal distinction? Now is the time for New Zealand to
show some courage of a new kind. We are on the Security Council. What are we doing
there? Why are we not making the most of our membershi p there? Why are we not
displaying our parliamentary interest in this by holding a debate specifically on the
subject of sending troops to Iraq?

items.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.role: Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs
items.text: It is
very good to be back in the House after a great summer, and to be part of a rejuvenated
and energetic team determined to do our best for New Zealand. We are determined to
carry on the strong, stable Government of the past 6 years that we have enjoyed and that
has steadily increased levels of confidence in this country.
Confidence lies at the core of so much progress. It is confidence that encourages
people to invest. It is confidence that encourag es people to start a new business and to
hire new workers. Many of the people in my neighbourhood, in the Epsom electorate,
are doing just that, and many other people around the country have had the confidence
to start new businesses and employ new people this year and over the past few years.
Confidence allows you to take the plunge from being on a benefit to going into a job,
trying a job, and tens of thousands of people have been doing that over the past year. It
is confidence that underpins higher aspir ations. People ask: “Is it possible for me to do
further training and go for a promotion?”. You need confidence, and that is what this
country has enjoyed in increasing levels over the past 6 years of this Government. My
goal is that we have at least anoth er 6 years of this Government in this country, and this
country will really sing.
There are a lot of new faces in this Chamber since the last election. The curious thing
is that most of the new faces are on this side of the Chamber. I suppose New Zealand
First has a number of new people from an interesting range of backgrounds, and I hope
that they will have the opportunity to make some positive contribution to New Zealand
over the years. There are 14 excellent new MPs on this side of the House from a wide
range of backgrounds —business people, doctors, farmers, and mayors of towns, who
have lots of new ideas and plenty of energy, and are grounded in the communities from
which they come. We have also seen a renewal in the executive, and I am pleased to be
part of that. There will be more about that later.
1570 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
So at the start of National’s 7 th year in Government, we have got a combination of
proven capability and experience with fresh determination and rejuvenation, and that is
a good place for any party to be. W e need it because the challenges facing this country
have not gone away. The fundamental economic challenge for New Zealand is about
continuing to become more internationally competitive in a world that never stands still.
That challenge is a huge one. It requires relentless effort, thought, and questioning of
the way we do things —from the quality of our education system to the impact of
regulation on the price of land and housing, the way we attract capital, the
competitiveness of domestic markets, and to so many other things. That international
competitiveness is absolutely one focus of this Government. It has been for the last 6
years and will continue to be. It is that international competitiveness that leads to higher
incomes. We all know that this is a n expensive time of the year, as kids are going back
to school. It is tough for families, and it is higher incomes that make life much more
enjoyable and that open up more opportunities for families in New Zealand. That is why
we work so hard to improve that international competitiveness.
Other fundamental challenges we face are making sure we remain plugged in to
international markets. That is why Tim Groser and the Government are working so hard
to continue to expand our trade relationships. The challenge remains also to continue to
do everything we can as a small country to bolster the rules -based international system
upon which we depend for our security and access to trade. We cannot take it for
granted that we will continue to operate in an essentiall y benign environment like we
have for so many decades. We have to continue to work hard to maintain old
friendships and to develop new ones. New Zealand has a great opportunity ahead of us
on the Security Council.
We have also got the challenge of the growing pains of Auckland. Particularly in
Auckland we need to continue to invest in infrastructure and to work hard to increase
the supply of land so that housing is affordable for people who live in that beautiful city.
We also have huge challenges that rem ain in the social sphere, and I am thrilled that we
have made so much progress in that area. I never thought that I would live to see the day
when I would see a New Zealand Herald article that said: “State of the nation: Life
getting better on most indicators”. Was that not a wonderful headline in the New
Zealand Herald yesterday? That was looking at the Salvation Army’s state of the nation
report, where it said we have been making significant progress in 14 out of the 22 social
indicators, and, actually, progress in a whole lot more. Child poverty is down, child
abuse is falling, early childhood education is going well, and teenage pregnancy has
dropped enormously over the last 5 years —down 15 percent in this year. That is so
important because we know that that group of teenage parents, if the resources are not
thrown into them, can remain on welfare for a very long time. So we are making great
progress in that area.
Crime is falling —serious crime is falling —the prison rate is falling, reoffending is
falling, real incomes are growing, employment is growing, and benefit numbers are
falling. So much progress is being made. But the point I would make is that this
Government is one that is proud of the progress that we have made so far over the past 6
years, but it is also keenly aware that there is so much more we can do. We are hungry
to get out and do that so we can continue to drive down crime rates in this country, so
we can continue to raise employment and get more and more people having the
opportunity to make a life for their families that is prosperous and good, so continue to
give people the opportunity to get off welfare and free themselves from the welfare
dependency that they have had for so long, and so we can continue to do the many sorts
of things that this Government has done over the past 6 years.
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1571
I want to talk briefly about some of the areas in the commerce and consumer affairs
portfolio. I am conscious, particularly in the financial markets area, that we have had a
very comprehensive set of reforms in the Financial Markets Conduct Act that have
come into place at the end of last year and that are aimed at increasing investor
confidence and improving access to capital, so that businesses can get that capital that
they need to grow. It has been a  very, very significant change, and lots of companies
have had to do a lot of work and will be doing a lot of work over the next couple of
years as we transition into the new regulatory regime. I will be making sure that the
Financial Markets Authority con tinues to work in a positive and open relationship with
the markets, as it does very successfully now, so that they can all work together
effectively under this new regime. We are also going to be looking at the financial
advisers review over the next 18 m onths, which we have signalled. We know that there
are a number of areas under the current legislation that could be working better, and I
am looking forward to hearing from the sector on this important issue so that we can
look at all the options to improve that area.
On the consumer side, we are working hard on putting the finishing touches together
on the Responsible Lending Code document that will provide high- level guidance to
help lenders adhere to regulations set out in the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance
Act. We know that most lenders are already following responsible lending practices
with their customers, and we encourage and support them, but we know that there is a
group—particularly loan sharks and some of the less responsible pay -day lenders—that
is not, and we want to make sure that we are doing all we can to protect those most
vulnerable members of society from being ripped off by some of the more unscrupulous
practitioners. But we are also conscious that we do not want to put too much e xtra
burden of red tape and overly prescriptive requirements on responsible lenders. So that
is a balancing act that we are working very hard to get right.
Both of those areas do touch on the wider issue of the effort that we are making
across the Governm ent to raise levels of financial capability across the community,
because we want to create a nation of investors. We have got 2.4 million people
enrolled in KiwiSaver. We encourage them to grow their wealth and we want them to
have access to good advice w hen they need it. So the financial advisers review is
considering the practice at the moment and seeing whether we can improve that. We
also recognise that that absence of basic money skills is one that can really compound
problems that the poorest familie s in New Zealand have. So the Responsible Lending
Code is one part of designing legislation to protect the most vulnerable, but there is also
a huge effort right across the Government in terms of educating and trying to lift levels
of financial literacy, a nd that will be very much a focus of this Government over the
next 3 years. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: There are many issues that could be
discussed during this debate —the housing crisis in Auckland or the Government’s
willingness to put $130 million into a profit -making casino but not into providing a
decent public transport system —but today I want to focus on foreign affairs. I want to
do so because tomorrow the Iraqi For eign Minister, Dr Ibrahim al- Jaafari, visits New
Zealand. There is no doubt this is a carefully stage -managed event. Dr al -Jaafari is
coming here because he has been asked to come here to formally request the assistance,
by way of boots on the ground, of N ew Zealand troops in Iraq. It will be so carefully
stage-managed that I can tell you now what the response of the Prime Minister will be:
“We have listened to his request and we will consider it carefully.” It will come as a
surprise to no New Zealander that this is simply designed to soften up public opinion for
the deployment of New Zealand soldiers to Iraq, which most New Zealanders over a
period of time will come strongly to oppose.
1572 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
You see, it really is a charade, because we know that the decision has  already been
taken by the Key Government to deploy New Zealand soldiers in Iraq. We know that,
notwithstanding the promise made by Mr Key before the election that there would be no
New Zealand ground troops in Iraq— a promise made and not reversed until sa fely after
the election. How do we know that the Government has already made the decision? We
know it because John Key told Tony Abbott. He told him that we would have 40 to 100
New Zealand troops committed to Iraq. At the same time, he was telling New
Zealanders that no decision was made. That is dishonest. He told the Australians, he
told the Americans, and Gerry Brownlee went and said it to the then Secretary of
Defence. John Key told the British but he did not tell New Zealanders.
John Key is treating New Zealanders with contempt. You know, I watched yesterday
during question time when he had a hard question to answer about differences of
opinion between Mr Joyce and Mr English, and he said that he would listen to both the
children. That was very patroni sing and you could see the looks on the faces of his
senior colleagues, but that is exactly what he is treating New Zealanders like —children.
They are not adult enough to know. We will tell them when they need to know, when
we actually have no time for deb ate, and the decision is already taken. In the United
Kingdom, of course, John Key went further. He was in a BBC interview —actually
being done by one of my former students, Lucy Hockings —and he was very upfront, in
a way that he is not in New Zealand. He s aid yes, we will be sending troops there,
notwithstanding the human costs, because that is the price of the club. For the first time
we got the real reason why we will be deploying New Zealand troops to Iraq and
putting them in harm’s way. It is not for human rights reasons, not even for the Islamic
State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), but because that is the price of being in the club.
That is the same club that John Key and Bill English wanted us to join in 2003 when
the United States launched the invasion of Iraq. I remember it well; I was Minister of
Foreign Affairs. I had Bill English ask me questions about why we were not supporting
the invasion, why we were not part of it, why we were not working with our friends and
allies, and John Key said exactly the same. I wonder whether they now think back with
shame about their comments, because history has proven that that invasion was not
simply a disaster that cost tens of thousands of human lives but a disaster based on a lie.
Colin Powell said to me when I was Minister of Foreign Affairs that the worst thing that
he ever did was to go to the UN Security Council and say that the United St ates invaded
because of weapons of mass destruction. I believe him; he was a decent and honourable
man. But that disaster spawned the existence of, and support for, ISIS today. Without
the 2003 invasion there would be no basis for ISIS to exist in Iraq. Th at was the price of
a decision made without thinking through the consequences, gung -ho—maybe for all
the right intentions; I do not know, but it was the wrong decision.
Every Western intervention in that region has ended up achieving the opposite of
what the objective was, whether it was Iraq or Libya. Libya is in absolute chaos at the
moment. Yes, it was easy to get rid of and easy to hate Gaddafi and Saddam Hussein.
They were evil, bad people. But what are the consequences of your actions? The West
has never learnt how to achieve good results other than by going in with guns blazing
and ending up achieving exactly the opposite, after enormous loss of human—and
mainly civilian —lives. John Key and Bill English were wrong in 2003 and they are
wrong now. They are doing the wrong thing for the wrong reason.
You know, New Zealanders do understand sacrifice. They understand that there are
times when we have to put ourselves on the line and that there are sometimes costs that
we have to pay for the preservation o f our society and our democracy. But what they
demand, quite rightfully, is to know that we are doing the right thing for the right
reason, that we have thought it through, and that there are achievable objectives that will
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1573
flow from the sacrifice that mig ht be made. We are not doing this for the right reason.
Gerry Brownlee was absolutely right in condemning as unfortunate his own Prime
Minister’s statement about being part of the club —very courageous, Minister, very
courageous. He backtracked very quickly , and maybe that was not a show of courage.
But the fact of the matter is that it is not the right thing to do, it is not for the right
reason, and, sadly, it will not achieve the objectives that we are looking for.
I heard the Prime Minister sounding qui te passionate about human rights in the
House this week. That is the first time ever I have heard him speak in that manner. But I
wonder where the Prime Minister was when it came to condemning the actions of
Bashar al-Assad, who has slaughtered more than 100,000 of his own people and, again,
created the foundation for the existence and the creation of ISIS in Syria. I wonder
where the National Government is on Boko Haram and condemnation of that. When I
hear the Prime Minister talking about beheadings, I wonder why he said not a word
about the routine stonings and beheadings under sharia law by Saudi Arabia. We
condemn, rightly, ISIS for beheadings—and we run the flag at half-mast for the King of
Saudi Arabia, who presides over a regime that kills in a bruta l way hundreds of people
for reasons and causes that would not even be against the law in our country.
There are some questions that should be put to Dr al -Jaafari, and they are these—and
I hope that the Minister of Defence and the Prime Minister ask thes e questions. Why
should we have confidence in putting New Zealanders at risk to go to Iraq when the
Iraqi army has performed so poorly? Why should we believe that we can make a
difference when the United States has invested $25 billion and thousands of Ame rican
trainers—to produce an army that remains corrupt, incompetent, and poorly led? Why is
it that the first time the Iraqi army went up against ISIS it collapsed and passed its
advanced American weapons to ISIS? Why is it that the Peshmerga have defeated  ISIS
in Kobani with a fraction of the support that the Iraqi army has been given? Why is it
that American money is being spent to fund 50,000 soldiers in Iraq who do not exist?
The money is being put into the pockets of the elite in Iraq. Why is it that they expect us
to do for the Iraqi army what the Iraqi army cannot and will not do for itself? Those are
the questions that John Key, Murray McCully, and Gerry Brownlee ought to be asking
Dr al-Jaafari tomorrow, and if there are not good answers to those questions, we should
not be putting New Zealand lives at risk for a futile purpose. Let us help with
humanitarian aid. The $30 million we will be spending on troops can do a lot for the 13
million refugees from not only ISIS but also al-Assad and the Shi’a and Sunni militias.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. Sarah
Dowie—5 minutes.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: What an opportunity it is to take this
call in support of the Prime Minister’s statement. I am so proud to be part of this John
Key and National -  led Government that has delivered on its promises to New
Zealanders. It is a Governm ent that has navigated this country through the global
financial crisis, all the while supporting the vulnerable, and still, within its third term,
has an ambitious programme to lock in the gains we have made and continue to grow
this country’s economy, to reduce unnecessary bureaucracy, to deliver better public
services, and to support ordinary Kiwis to achieve their hopes and dreams. New
Zealand, the country that we live in and we thrive in, will continue to be the envy of the
rest of the world.
I want t o take this time to talk about our competitive economy, which is creating
more jobs, which is raising incomes and providing more opportunities for our people.
What better way to highlight this than to talk about Southland—sensational Southland,
sunny Southland, Sarah’s Southland. Did you know that according to the Business and
1574 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
Economic Research Ltd report of November 2014 that as a region Southland produces
15 percent of New Zealand’s total exports, including value-added products?

items.speaker: Stuart Smith
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: 15 percent. One of the goals of the Business Growth Agenda is
for all New Zealand regions to apply a 40 percent ratio of GDP to exports. Southland
already has a ratio of 70 percent of our GDP to exports, predominant ly in the primary
value-added industry. That makes Southland the food bowl of New Zealand. Through
the opening of markets with our free -trade agreements, largely in China, we can sell
more of our goods. Production is high and we can increase. We have jobs —3.2 percent
unemployment.

items.speaker: Stuart Smith
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: 3.2 percent. In fact, local economic agencies are forecasting
ongoing demand in the trades, technology, and service sectors, so there will be jobs in
the future. The median house price in Invercargill is $186,000, against the New Zealand
median of $450,000—come on down. Southland produces nearly $53,000 of GDP per
head, the third highest in the country behind Taranaki’s oil and gas production and
Wellington’s policy production, according to the regional economic activity report of
2014 from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. Southland is the best
in the country when it comes to affordable house rentals. And guess what! In
Invercargill we do not have traffic jams. We officially have a rush minute.
But we will not rest there. We are ambitious as we move into the future. Diversifying
our economy is important to building resilience in an export -driven economy. We have
opportunities, thanks to the potenti al of platinum and silica —sensible resource
development supported by a John Key – led Government. We have the Southern
Institute of Technology offering everything from free trade courses to a Bachelor of
Commerce, and, of course, zero fees.
There are plen ty of reasons to live in Southland. One of them is that Southland
responds well to responsible, fiscally savvy, and forward- thinking Governments like
this National- led one. We will create policy and macroeconomic tools to ensure
Southland, Invercargill, and any other parts of New Zealand that want to work as hard
as us Southlanders will have the opportunities to do so and to create more wealth, jobs,
and chances.
This team on the centre to centre- right is a united one. Our Prime Minister is
inspiring, our Ministers are brilliant, and our members are passionate about the regions
they represent and this country. We will work together and we will continue to deliver
for the people of New Zealand now and in the future.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Barbara Kuriger—5 minutes.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: What a privilege
it is to be in  the House at the start of what is shaping up to be a fantastic 2015. The
Government is one that is constantly making leaps and bounds in all sectors. We are
working for families across the board, in business, health care, social welfare, housing
affordability, and unemployment, all with the end goal of a more prosperous future for
everyone in New Zealand.
It is pleasing to see that the world -class broadband network is kicking off to a great
start this year. Ultra -fast broadband targets are well ahead of s chedule, with 40 percent
of planned infrastructure projects now complete. More than half a million New Zealand
homes are now connected to fibre broadband, with over 2,000 schools able to connect to
ultra-fast broadband.
Yesterday it was announced that 14 new Rural Broadband Initiative towers have
been completed, which means extended cellphone coverage for the remote areas of New
Zealand, making it easier to deal with emergencies, transport logistics, and road safety
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1575
issues. The Government is investing $300  million in the Rural Broadband Initiative,
with the same level of investment from partners, meaning high -speed wireless
broadband to enhance communities in some of our remotest parts of the country.
One of the biggest jump- starts to come from the impleme ntation of these broadband
towers is the boost to New Zealand’s rural economy. That will occur by enabling those
in our community the use of the latest farming technology and agri -innovation. As a
farmer I know how important it is to be able to track fertiliser, irrigation, and rainfall.
Digital communication, enhanced by good internet, enables this to happen. Reliable
access to the network at home and at work on these high -speed networks means more
employment, more study options for young people, higher business productivity with
access to online services, and the ability for rural businesses to connect with markets
and customers in other parts of New Zealand and overseas. One of the essential benefits
of faster broadband is the better access to health care that comes with it, which I know
many New Zealanders in rural communities will be thrilled about.
Rural broadband highlights the Government’s continual commitment to connecting
the rural to the urban and helping to close the divide that has been a little  bit separated
over recent years. It will provide faster broadband to 90 percent of our homes. I recently
visited a programme where children in a North Island rural school —really remote —
have a programme now whereby they are Skypeing children in the South I sland. It is
seeing results like this that reinforces the message of what the Government is doing.
Our Prime Minister’s statement on Tuesday identified a key point in the
Government’s policy agenda for this year and that is to build a more competitive and
productive economy, and this is happening and it is happening now. New Zealand is
doing well compared with other countries. Our economy is growing, employment is
increasing, and wages are rising. Investment and exports make a stable basis for the
expanding economy that our nation has. At the forefront of our measures for a
competitive and productive economy are our game -changing trade agreements,
including negotiating the Trans -Pacific Partnership where we can rest assured that the
Government is ensuring that the total best interests of New Zealand are being served.
This Government was recently elected again by the people of New Zealand for many
reasons and one of these was to ensure a better future for all Kiwis. New Zealanders
elected us because they kno w we have a track record of delivering results. No matter
how many disparaging comments the other side of the House throws at us, Kiwis know
that this Government is implementing measures that are putting New Zealand on the
map in the international trade ma rket. We are increasing exports and subsequently
increasing the quality of capital for those Kiwi- owned family businesses that are now
open to more channels of exports.
In rural regions such as Taranaki - King Country roading projects are welcome news
and will lead to greater accessibility and safer roads to travel on, reducing the number of
accidents. Awakino Gorge has been prioritised as a focus for the Government to
improve safety in this area, and as an MP I am really excited about this. So we are
delivering outstanding results in 2015 and beyond, and I am looking forward to the
future. Thank you.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: I want to start by congratulating the
leader and the dep uty leader of the Labour Party on a fabulous job that they have done
since the end of last year. Does my team not agree that they have done a great job? I
want to say this to members on the other side. Prepare for that day after election day in
2017, because we know what the headline will be. The day after the election in 2017 it
will be “A Little goes a long way”. I guarantee you that on that day after the election
you will be staring down the barrel of a Labour Government, so please be prepared. We
are excited. You should be too, because I am sure the rest of New Zealand is as well.
1576 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: I am sorry. I am not saying that you will be excited, Mr
Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I may well be, but you are
not allowed to bring me into the debate. Thank you.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: Sure.
From so many members on the other side of the House we have heard about the
economic management credentials of the National Government. I just want to say that
actually it is not economic management that the National Government members are
good at; it is the creation of the perception that they are great economic managers that
they are good at. There was an interesting question put to the Government earlier today
and it brought up the fact that the Prime Minister dropped the ball six times when
getting filmed for a Cricket World Cup promo. Dropping the ball six times —that is
quite a good image, because I was thinking about the fact that that Government has
dropped the ball more than six times with regard to its economic management and
financial management of this country.
Let me just give you six examples of where the National Government has failed New
Zealand in terms of its economic management and financial decision -making. Let us
start just with a fairly recent one and that would be the Skycity convention centre. What
did the Government tell us? It told us and it told New Zealand that this would not cost
us a cent. And what are we looking at now —$130 million on the taxpayer. That is not
the promise, that is not the assurance, that the National Government gave to the country
when the deal was done and signed. But here we are, with the financial gurus over there
costing the taxpayers $130 million that was not budgeted for.
No. 2 in terms of examples of the great financial management of the National
Government is that we were told when National first got into office that it would close
the wage gap with Australia. And what was the wage gap at that time —$121.76. Did it
manage to close that wage gap with Australia? Well, actually, no. The wage gap is now
$170.28. Is that a good example of good economic management by the National
Government?

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: They’ve dropped the ball.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: National has dropped the ball twice. Two examples of
where it has dropped the ball.
Another good example is a case that all New Zealanders are very aware of and that is
Novopay. How much did Novopay cost us? Well, it cost us $110 million just to set up
and run and then it cost us an additional $45 million to fix. Then, on top of that, Steven
Joyce made the decision not only to maintain the flawed system but then to buy the
flawed system on behalf of the taxpayer. I am sure New Zealanders are looking at the
National Government and thinking “Great economic managers.” That is the third
example of dropping the ball.
The fourth example I would like to share with the House goes to exports. We heard
some of the members on that side of the House talking about how great the National
Government has done in terms of exports. Now let us look at the facts. National
members said they would increase exports from 30 percent to 40 percent of GDP, but
instead now the figure is down under 30 percent and still going down. They are four
examples of where the National Government, like its Prime Minister —with its Prime
Minister—has dropped the ball.
No. 5, a great example of the financial management of the gurus on the other side of
the House, is that the National Government flogged off our State assets and did not get
the money it expected, including from the sale of Meridian Energy, which it sold for $1
per share to 2 percent of New Zealanders and now those shares are trading for $2 per
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1577
share. Is that a good example of great management? That is the fifth example of
dropping the ball. The sixth one I would li ke to share is the surplus that that
Government was anticipating making, but now what we have is Treasury forecasting
that National will be $572 million short of the surplus that it told New Zealand it would
reach.
So, unfortunately for New Zealand, it is  not that National members are great
economic managers and good with our economy; it is the fact that they have been so
good at pulling the wool over New Zealand’s eyes and creating the perception that they
are good economic managers. The six examples I have just shared with you, where
National has dropped the ball, paint a pretty clear picture that it is irresponsible with
taxpayers’ money, and, actually, it is completely incompetent when it comes to financial
management of any sort. So I think that over the next 2½ years New Zealand is going to
become more aware of these examples of where National has dropped the ball. There
are going to be more places —because National members cannot help themselves —
where they will drop the ball. Actually, what we are increasingly seeing when we go out
and about and meet the public is that people are becoming increasingly concerned. So,
National members, please do not get too comfortable in those seats and maintain the
level of arrogance we are seeing too often as we are ou t and about and even here in the
House, because what we do know is that politics goes in cycles, and that New
Zealanders are becoming increasingly aware of the National Government’s shortfalls.
I want to refer to another thing that I am really concerned about, and that is the
banter that we have had from the other side of the House towards our leader about his
desire to focus on the future of work in New Zealand. One thing that has been apparent
for many years is that Labour actually does look to the future. Labour actually does plan
for the future. Labour looks down the track and thinks about what we need to do to
prepare our country for the future. There are some very clear examples of where
National has dropped the ball with regard to preparation, and I just want to point out a
couple of those. One of those —because we have heard so much about the rebuild in
Christchurch—is that when National first got into office in 2008 one of the first
decisions it made was to cut funding from trades training. Now we ha ve National
members constantly talking about the fact that we have a shortfall of skilled
tradespeople to undertake the work. National members are so quick to forget that
actually one of the first places they made cuts was in trades training.
The second p oint I would like to make in respect of where National did not look to
the future, and made irresponsible decisions, was with regard to some of the decisions it
made in our schools. Today I looked in the newspaper and I saw one of the Ministers
reporting on the fact that National wants to put a focus on the obesity problem that we
have in this country. Yes, that is a very important issue to focus on and a place to put
some resource, but, actually, when National first got into office, what did it do? It
actually cut out —I do not know why —the healthy food in schools policy. So I think
that National needs to spend some time reflecting on the irresponsible decisions that
have been made. I guarantee that New Zealanders are looking at some of the decisions
that have been made, looking at some of the statements that have been made now, and
finding it really difficult to reconcile the actions it has taken in the past and the
statements it is making at present.
If I go back to the future of work stuff, I totally get behind, like everyone else here,
our leader with the need to focus on the future of work. We have so many issues in
terms of unemployment. The figure for the last quarter was 5.4 percent, and now we are
at 5.7 percent. Unemployment is not going down under this Government. This
Government is irresponsible in terms of our economic management and New
Zealanders are suffering because of it.
1578 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand that  it is the
intention of the National Party to split the next two calls.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Happy New Year, Mr Assistant
Speaker Mallard, and happy New Year to my parliament ary colleagues. I am looking
forward to a great year in 2015: a great year in the House, a great year in the region of
Canterbury, and a great year in my electorate of Waimakariri.
The Prime Minister started his excellent speech on Tuesday morning by talk ing
about jobs. He talked about incomes, and he talked about supporting families. I went to
hear the Salvation Army’s state of the nation report yesterday morning, and I was
interested in the fact that during the presentation the organisation showed a line  graph
that was tracking downwards, and that was child poverty. So, as the curious new, young
MP I am, I put my hand up and I asked Alan Johnson, who wrote the report, why child
poverty is tracking down. His response was: “Job creation.” There you go —job creation
reduces child poverty, and this National Government has created 80,000 new jobs in the
last year and will create 150,000 new jobs in the next 2 years. Can I remind the
Opposition members that the last state of the nation report by the Salvation Arm y when
they were in Government in 2008 said that for all their increased expenditure they did
not increase social progress by 1 percent.
The Prime Minister also spoke on Tuesday about the Canterbury earthquake
recovery. The earthquake recovery is a big and key focus of mine, as I have a
background in health, specifically in mental health. I am not talking just about bricks
and mortar when I talk about recovery. International research will show us that years 3
to 5 are the most problematic for psychological and social recovery, and I think we need
to remind ourselves that it is not the Christchurch earthquake and rebuild; it is the
Canterbury earthquakes and rebuild. A town in my electorate, Kaiapoi, was hit severely
by the first earthquakes in September 2010. So I would like to remind people about the
Canterbury District Health Board’s All Right? campaign. It is worth repeating that it is
all right to ask for help, and I would ask my parliamentary colleagues to ensure we
continue to focus on the Canterbury e arthquake recovery in 2015 and provide the
support that Cantabrians need.
The year 2015 is going to be a great year of milestones and new beginnings in
Canterbury. I opened last month, with the Mayor of Waimakariri, David Ayers, the
Ruataniwha Kaiapoi Civic Centre, which has a new library of 30,000 books, a museum,
and an art space. It was built using technology that will see the building last well into
the future. It is a good example of local and central government working together with
the local communi ty to build an anchor project that is a symbol of recovery and a
symbol of the way we are heading in the future. I am proud to be part of a Government
that believes in community facilities, strong families, and caring communities. The
Government gave a grant to the Waimakariri District Council of $7 million, and $1.5
million of that was used towards this new library development. The year 2015 is going
to be a great year of milestones and new beginnings in the Canterbury earthquake
recovery. In the next mont h we will open the Rangiora and Oxford town halls. We will
open the Ashley Bridge. The North Canterbury Health Hub will open up in the middle
of the year, and my constituents are looking forward to first -class health care facilities
on their doorstep. We w ill be starting $300 million of roading projects, which will
reduce commuter congestion, and the future use of red-zoned land will be decided.
But tonight the eyes of the world will be on Christchurch with the International
Cricket Council  Cricket World C up opening. At the start of the year I watched the
Black Caps beat Sri Lanka at the new Hagley Oval, and it was impressive as I watched
the crowd—because Cantabrians love their sport. It was a hot nor’wester day and they
were enjoying this new sporting fac ility. It was great to see one of the Canterbury
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1579
anchor recovery projects being so successful, and now we have, arguably, the best
cricket ground in New Zealand.
Can I say that the Government is continuing to stand beside the people of Canterbury
as good progress is made on the earthquake rebuild. The year 2015 is going to be a year
of milestones and new beginnings in the Canterbury recovery. Thank you.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Tēnā koe, e te Mana Whakawā. I rise to support the
motion, but, firstly, I want to acknowledge the passing of two great leaders of

items.speaker: Māoridom
items.text: Apirana Mahuika of Ngati Porou and Tama Huata of Ngāti Kahungunu. Nō
reira, e ngā rakatira haere atu rā, haere atu  rā. Haere atu rā ki te pao o te whakawairua,
takoto mai, takoto. [ And so, to the esteemed elders, go forth; farewell. Depart to the
spiritual beat. Lie there, rest.] Let the dead be the dead and the living be the living.
I want to highlight one thing that  the Prime Minister said in his speech: National is a
Government doing something for Māori. One of the reasons I sought to enter Parliament
as a National MP was to advance the cause of Māori. Some of my people have
expressed scepticism and asked how I coul d join National. These are the people who
buy in to the widespread perception that the party opposite is the one that can do the
most for our people. Let me be clear. I joined the National Party because it is the party
that has done the most for Māori in the past and will do the most for Māori in the future.
It is indeed about aspirations. For too long Māori have been at the bottom of many
major social indicators —in particular, education and welfare dependency. For too long
Māori have looked for Labour to t urn things round. For too long Labour has let our
people down.
Labour is full of rhetoric on the importance of education. From what I have seen and
heard, the Māori MPs on the other side of the House really care about our people and
the importance of a good education. They talk a good game, but when it comes time to
stand up and do something about the problems that exist, it is the teachers unions that
get the final say. Labour’s answers to educational underachievement have been to
ignore the failing schools, to oppose telling parents how their children are doing, and to
fight against innovation in our education system. Our whānau want their kids to
succeed. So when National says we should help parents to be more involved in their
child’s learning, they welc ome that. They welcome being told in plain language how
their children are doing. They welcome having data available that shows how their
children’s school is performing. They agree with the Government that schools should be
operating in the interests of their students and not those of the teachers union bosses.
The fact that National is good for Māori is evident from the settlement of historic
Treaty claims. As the Prime Minister said in his speech, Labour signed only one or two
deeds of settlement per year. But now, just after over 6 years of a National Government,
we have signed 46 deeds of settlement. That is fantastic progress and it makes me proud
to represent National.
I want to acknowledge our relationship with the Māori Party. Together, we have
improved social outcomes for Māori through Whānau Ora, and we have repealed Helen
Clark’s land -grab of the foreshore and seabed. This Government remains relentlessly
focused on lifting the living standards of Māori, along with every other New Zealander,
through economic growth. Labour’s approach to Māori in poverty has been to keep
them there. Labour talks about jobs and lifting our people out of poverty, and when the
time has come to act, it has done nothing. On this side of the House we know what it
takes to lift people out of poverty. It is not sitting around talking about what a job is. It
is not voting against every single job -creating measure this Government has put in
place. It is not burdening small businesses with red tape and higher taxes and still
expecting them to take on one more staff member.
1580 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
National has restored confidence in our economy, which was crippled by the global
recession and a Labour Government. Businesses now have the confidence to take on
new workers thanks to the 90- day trial period. As I said at the beginning of my speech,
this is about aspirations.
I live on a papatupu, or an ancestral community. This is the Māori heartland. I can
tell the Leader of the Opposition that most Māori do not want to talk about self -
governance. Our aspirations as a people are much higher than that. Like everyone else,
Māori care about education, we care about jobs, and we care about the welfare of our
children. We are not interested in the sort of separatism that is around the self -
governance talk from the other side. What we are interested in is an ongoing partnership
with the Crown that will enable us as a people to fulfil our aspirations. The Opposition
parties will say anything to get into Government, but empowering our people to reach
the future they as pire to is, again, about walking the talk. If I could sum up Labour’s
achievements for Māori in one sentence, it would be this: after all that was said and
done, there was more said than done. Kia ora.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Just before I call the next
member, and I think we have just had a fairly egregious example of it, I do want to warn
members that in this debate it is not appropriate to read speeches.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: It is with pleasure that I rise to take part in
this debate on the Prime Minister’s statement. I am really proud to be part of t his team
in Government, because when the National -led Government presented its first Budget,
in 2009, it did so against the backdrop of a sharp recession that began in early 2008 and
the impact of the worst global financial crisis since the 1930s. In the a bsence of policy
change, the outlook was going to be endless debt and exploding levels of Government
debt. On top of this, New Zealand experienced the Canterbury earthquakes and a series
of finance company failures.
So the Government’s plan throughout thi s period was to support the economy in the
short term by running operating deficits, reflecting lower tax revenue and higher
spending on items such as benefits. This approach of the Government provided that
extra support to the economy when it was needed t he most, and cushioned New
Zealanders and their families in the recession when this was required. However, the
Government did so within a clear framework of helping Kiwis get ahead and getting net
Government debt below 20 percent by 2020. Now, our GDP grow th is among the
highest in the OECD, and is expected to average almost 3 percent over the next 5 years.
New Zealand is doing well compared with most other countries. Interest rates are
staying lower for longer. Household disposable income is rising faster  than inflation,
rising by 9 percent in real terms in the last 4 years, and is forecast to increase by another
9 percent over the next 4 years. Unemployment is forecast to drop to 4.5 percent by
2018. Employment is growing. Yes, employment is growing. Eighty thousand more
people are employed than a year ago, and 217,000 more people are employed than 5
years ago. This Government knows how to create the environment where businesses can
prosper and have the confidence of investing more in their businesses and employing
more staff. New Zealand recorded 3.9 percent economic growth over the year to June,
which was one of the higher rates among developed countries.
The New Zealand economy provides an amazing opportunity for businesses and
investments. The investme nt opportunities are endless. New Zealand is recognised
globally as being a safe place to invest and do business. We are growing new industries,
such as information and communications technology and high- tech manufacturing, and
strengthening existing ones, such as the food industry, tourism, and international
education. And we are making strides in areas such as welfare, education, health, and
law and order, to help improve the lives of New Zealanders and their families. I cannot
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1581
