express how thrilled the communities in Mount Roskill and around Auckland get when I
tell them about the National Government’s HomeStart package, which will be up and
running from 1 April this year. It will help around 90,000 homebuyers into their first
house over the next 5 years. What I hear from wider communities when I am out and
about is that the National -led Government is a Government that delivers what we said
we would. Yes, the National -led Government is a Government that delivers what we
said we would.
My own very recent experience— I am still in the process of looking for a suitable
space to lease out and set up my out -of-Parliament office, but there is a very small
number of vacant commercial properties, and then they are not available in the area I am
keen on. Despite this being a little time-consuming, it does provide a perspective of how
good our economy is doing at the moment. This is because nearly all commercial
buildings are occupied by businesses that are finding a high level of success. Such a
high occupancy of commercial buildings is a practical sign of a brilliant economy.
This Government, under the leadership of the Rt Hon John Key, is working in the
interests of every New Zealander. Under a National Government, New Zealand is in
good shape and is getting bette r. This is due to the hard work and positive attitude of
New Zealanders. It is also because of the stability and confidence that have come from 6
years of a strong and stable Government. We are taking the next steps to lock in the
gains of the last 6 years, to create a long-term lift in New Zealand’s prosperity. There is
much to do, as we have heard from the Prime Minister and Ministers, and we have 3
busy years ahead of us. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Can I say that it is exciting to be associated with a
Government that is getting on and getting things done. I found it kind of interesting to
hear from the last speaker from the opposite benches, who decided she would try to
accuse us of dropping the ball, yet at the last election ours was not the party that
dropped a seat. In fact, ours was a party that actually grew. And why did we grow?
Well, we grew, in terms of the majority that we had, because New Zealanders liked
what they saw over the last 6 years. They liked what this Government was doing and
they wanted more of it. They saw that there was something that they could be confident
in, and so they returned this National Government to the Treasury benches.
And why did they do it? Well, I can tell  you that the people I speak to on the streets
every day in Palmerston North have told me that it is because they have got confidence
in this Government and they have got confidence in this Prime Minister and in the
Minister of Finance. They have proved themselves worthy of the trust of the people of
New Zealand because they are getting things moving and New Zealand is improving.
But our work here is not finished. There is more for us to do. Although we are not
making Mainland cheese, good things do take some time, so we will continue to work
hard to continue to progress to ensure that New Zealand is moving forward.
There have been calls from the opposite side, as we have been talking about social
housing, that we should simply leave it alone. Well, I want to tell you a story from my
experiences in Palmerston North to explain just exactly why we should not leave social
housing alone. Last year, while campaigning, during the campaign, I was speaking to
somebody down at the markets —at the Albert Street Market,  in fact—who told me that
she was a Housing New Zealand tenant and had been in her house for about 30 years. I
thought “Well, that’s good.” She clearly needed the assistance of the New Zealand
people to be able to remain in that house. She said that she was income tested and so she
had to pay only $80 a week for her house. I thought “Well, if that’s her situation and
what she can afford, then perhaps it’s appropriate that that’s what she pays.” She told
me that her children had left home and that she was now living in her four -bedroom
1582 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
house. But do not worry; those rooms were not going to waste, because those rooms
were being occupied by overseas students, who were paying board to this person.
It was all above board, to be honest, because if you have two boa rders you do not
have to declare the income. In fact, you could argue that it was very entrepreneurial on
her part. But actually, as I was talking to her, I could not help but think of the stories
that we are all told and we hear about and have come across , of families with three or
more children who are perhaps living in overcrowded conditions because there is not
enough housing for them or appropriate housing for them to occupy. I thought perhaps
they would make better use of that house than international  students lining the pockets
of somebody who was, to be fair, making a profit on the back of hard- working New
Zealanders who are paying taxes and who are, perhaps, more deserving of that house.
Although I am not saying that we should just simply evict people from those houses, we
do need to engage more with them and ensure that we are monitoring them, and looking
to ensure that the resources that we have for our social housing in New Zealand are
actually being used in the most appropriate way.
Yesterday Ho using New Zealand came to the Social Services Committee to talk
about the year in review. It is very clear that we have got greater demand for certain
types of housing in certain places around New Zealand and less demand in other places.
Therefore, it is time something was done to rectify to that. So that is what we are doing.
That is what our Minister for Social Housing is doing. She has outlined her plans to do
that. She has outlined that we are not simply going to put people in houses and leave
them alone for 30 years. We are going to look for new ways to manage this. We are
going to engage with community organisations, which might, perhaps, for this person
have moved her on to a point where she did not need social housing any more.
So we have a plan. We  are going to support more New Zealanders into housing that
meets their needs. We are going to ensure that they can start to move towards
independence. We are going to increase the affordable housing supply, particularly in
Auckland. We have got a plan. We  are working towards it. New Zealand will be the
better for another 3 years of this National Government.

items.speaker: ADRIAN RURAWHE
items.text: Tēnā koe e Te Māngai o Te
W’are e tū ake nei, otirā, tika ana kia huri atu ki a rātau, ā, ki a rāua ta’i kua wehe atu ki
tua o te ārai. Nō reira, e te rangatira Api Mahuika, e te rangatira Tama Huata, tēnei a’au
e tuku mi’i poroporoaki ki a kōrua, haere atu rā. Nō reira, huri atu au ki Te Whare nei,
tēnā koutou, tēnā tātau.
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker of this House standing before us, but at the same time
it is fitting that I turn to the departed and to the two who have gone beyond the divide.
So to you both, esteemed elders Api Mahuika and Tama Huata, I bid you farewell and
goodbye. I turn now to you in this House, to acknowledge you and us collectively.]
It is a great privilege and pleasure for me to stand up today and join in this debate on
the Prime Minister’s statement to this House.  I am speaking against the motion and for
the amendment moved by the leader of the Labour Party, Andrew Little. Sometimes I
am told that I drop Māori words into my speeches and it is too quick, before people can
get a translation—one or two words. The thre e or four words that I am going to use in
my speech today —one is tino, which means very or really; rawa atu, which means
beyond or to the extremities of the word that precedes it; and, the third word that I am
going to use is hōhā, which means tiresome, bothersome, or fed up. Before I get into my
speech, those are the three words that I am going to use in this speech.
It was a great pleasure for me to stand and welcome all of the political parties to
Rātana Pā on 23 January this year. Everyone looked refreshed. I kept it fairly non-
partisan, because that is what the kaupapa of our marae there is; but in this House not so
much. I am going to address some of the issues that I have heard in the House today.
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1583
But before I do I want to touch on our visit to Waitangi. At Waitangi our Labour caucus
went on to Te Tii Marae and we were warmly welcomed there. Interestingly enough, we
went on to the marae after the Government parties. It was really unusual, because I have
been to a lot of mara es and I have attended many, many pōwhiri , and I know when the
local people are happy and when they are not happy. I know that the people who
welcomed us there, on to that marae, genuinely and sincerely expressed their affection
towards Andrew Little, the leader of the Labour Party. That is a fact. I also heard the
word “arrogant” three times from three different speakers on the home side, and they
were all referring to the Prime Minister —each and every one of them. They were not
happy with what he had said and the way he had said it. In fact, they were hōhā. They
were tino hōhā. Actually, they were tino hōhā rawa atu. That is a fact. They said to us
quite clearly on the marae, when welcoming us, that they were sick and tired of the way
that this Government has been talking to them and treating them. I think it is really
important that we say it in this House so that members on the Government benches can
hear it quite clearly. That is my message to the Government.
I will tell you something else. Flippant ans wers are being given in this House, or
actually not being given —a case in point was yesterday, when a Minister was on his
feet, not answering the question. On the cross benches every single National MP had
their head down. Indeed, I would say they were hōhā, and quite rightly so. I expect that
perhaps the senior Government whip might be sending out an email next week, because
during question time I think they will have their heads up this time. But that is an
indication that within the National Party member s, the National Government, there are
probably new members sitting there who know very well that those questions are not
being addressed in a way that is expected by the wider community who are watching. I
think our people who are watching here tonight and listening to the answers at question
time deserve an answer. Those answers are not coming. That is adding to their “hōhā -
ness”, if I can add an English ending to that word—their “hōhā -ness”. They are very
hōhā. They are also hōhā with the Māori Party. Tha t is why Labour doubled its number
of Māori electorate seats. That is a fact —that is a fact. And I encourage the National
MPs, because they do it all the time, to continue to tell the whole world how good a
relationship they have with the Māori Party, beca use guess what? Every time they do it
we get more votes. So I encourage the National MPs to continue doing that. Probably, I
should not have said that because they might actually stop, but I do not think that they
will. I think they will carry on because they need the Māori Party votes to do things like
end debates. So those sorts of motions where they might be against the bill but they vote
for the procedural motion to stop the debate are the things that our people —my people
out in the electorate—are telli ng me they do not like. So my message is, you know —
sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker—that one—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Ha, ha! He’s forgotten the message.

items.speaker: ADRIAN RURAWHE
items.text: No, I used the word “you” and I should not have. Sorry, Mr
Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: He was naughty, even if the
member did not recognise it. All right?

items.speaker: ADRIAN RURAWHE
items.text: So, our people are telling me that the y are sick and tired of
that kind of behaviour.
The important thing for me and for my Labour Party colleagues, and indeed our
Māori caucus colleagues —we have a strong Māori voice within the Labour Party —is
that Andrew Little, our leader, and others within the party have acknowledged the huge
responsibility and confidence that Māori have given back to Labour. We will stand up
to be a strong voice within this House and within this Parliament, despite what people
on the opposite side have said during this debate. Indeed, I was a bit taken aback by one
1584 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
Nuk Korako, who seemed to be telling us that National knows how to deal with poverty.
Really? Our people are really hōhā with that because, actually, the number of our people
living in poverty has grown, not reduc ed—grown. And there is all of the rhetoric
coming from that side of the House and from within the Prime Minister’s statement—
another example would be that the average income has increased. Well, if you actually
have a look at the statistics, those people e arning over $1,300 per week, certainly, their
incomes have increased significantly, but the incomes of the ones earning in the middle,
between $480 and $720 per week, have gone up by hardly anything. And for the ones
on the lowest income there have been ve ry modest increases. So that tells us that the
rich are continuing to get richer and the poor are staying where they are. My message to
the constituency across this nation is that we have the ideas, we have the team, we have
the leader, and I believe that at the next election we will be the Government and the
hōhā that exists today amongst our people will come to an end. N ō reira, tēnā koutou
katoa.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Can I start the year by saying
happy New Year to everyone—all our parliamentary colleagues and yourself, Mr
Assistant Speaker.
Su’a William Sio: Happy New Year, Judith.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Thank you very much. I have to say that after that
blistering attack from the member who has just resumed his seat, I should be feeling
some trepidation, but I am going to overcome that in the spirit of Parliament.

items.speaker: The ASSISTAN T SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I regret that I am
interrupting the member —and I will start her time again —but I am meant to say that
this is a split call. It is a 5-minute speech.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: We’re a split personality.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Ha, ha! Yes, we are splitting this with my colleague the
Hon Maurice Williamson, which I think is so appropriate.
Well, we have started the year quite interestingly. I think one of the great things in
the speeches from the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition was the tone.
Actually, Mr Andrew Little has been leader of the Labour Party for a matter of a few
months, and he was actually doing OK before Christmas. He was doing so OK that
many in the media were writing him up as the next best thing, and I am sure Labour
thought that it had finally found someone it could support. [ Interruption] Well, he was
pretty much the only other person standing who had not put their name up for some sort
of role, and the real leader of the Labour Party, the Hon Annette King, was not available
to take on the title.
But, having said that, what happened to him? He got a rush of blood to the head, and
I have been wondering why he would have started talking about Māori s overeignty and
getting everybody excited. Certainly, in Papakura people are concerned about this new
separatist movement that he seems to be wanting to promote. I thought: “What has gone
wrong with Andrew Little?”, because I am actually quite fond of him—no, I really am; I
am always fond of leaders of the Opposition because I think it is a good opportunity for
them to show their stripes, and it is good to do that —and I have worked it out: it is the
circadian rhythms. I did not know about circadian rhythms until Mr Little gave his first
media interview after he became the Leader of the Opposition, and he was late. He was
late because he does not believe in alarm clocks because of his circadian rhythms. So I
guess on Waitangi Day his circadian rhythms were a b it out because he had to get up
early.
I have got a bit of news for him, and it is that if he wants to be the leader of this
country, he is going to have to work out his circadian rhythms, because you cannot get
up at 5 o’clock in the morning and then go a nd talk about Māori sovereignty and
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1585
separatism and think that the people of New Zealand are going to think that that is a
good idea. I can tell you that Papakura is just all agog with it. I have to say that I am
going to talk a bit more about that in Papak ura over the next 3 years, and I think quite a
few people on this side of the House are going to help Mr Little remember the circadian
rhythms and why he should be focused on the things that are actually important for
Kiwis.
One of the things that is reall y important—which the Prime Minister spoke about,
and I have ad nauseam spoken and written about —is the need for Resource
Management Act reform. When I was practising law, before the Resource Management
Act even came in—oh, I know, I was a child genius! I know, Mr Assistant Speaker, that
you do not believe for a moment that I could be that old. But, yes, I was practising law
even when you were first an MP. I remember when the Resource Management Act
came in. It was almost like a light had come on. What happ ened is all these town
planners—who were then town planners —these fabulously experienced people, seemed
to leave Auckland City and go out as consultants. That is what I was dealing with a lot.
That is when we should always get concerned —when legislation le ads a lot of very
experienced, good, hard-working, skilled people to suddenly leave their jobs to become
consultants. That tells us there is something going on. So when we try to set up these
sorts of systems—I think with all the best of intentions—it unfortunately becomes a real
muddle.
I had that experience just last year when getting some work done at our home in
Maraetai. Many people will know about it; it has been on Campbell Live . They had a
good look through my wardrobe, which I felt was mildly invas ive, but there you go.
What we found was that with our little bridge, our walkway, we spent more money on
resource consent than we did on building the bridge. I think, unfortunately, that that is
just a little tale, but, actually, that is what is happening . We need to free up land, we
need to free up people to make good decisions, and we actually need to be able to have
faith in our builders and in the people who are developing land. One of the things in
Auckland in particular—because that is where most of the issues are around housing —
is that it is really about this metropolitan urban limit, which was put in place about 15
years ago. It has made it very expensive and difficult to actually get any new land
brought in for housing, and it has been like that for about 10 or 15 years. This is what
the developers are saying to me: “Sort this stuff out. Stop trying to impose limits on
people and actually have some faith in them.” Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I first want to say a
great big thankyou to our party whips for having let me get a speaking slot at this time
of day. My adoring drive time audience in Auckland, who will be crawling home at a
snail’s pace and taking an hour or an hour and a half to go only 15 to 20 kilometres, will
all be listening with bated breath. But I have got only a short slot, and in a short slot it is
wise to stick to only one subject. I was going to get into the rhythm method that Judith
Collins has been talking about. I think that the rhythm method is obviously what Labour
has been applying for some time. It is not working, and Labour needs to look for
something else.
I want to give Labour some advice. I have done this befo re, during drive time on
Radio Live and so on, and Labour does not seem to listen to that, but I am going to do it
again. It is really simple —it is really simple. The voting public actually vote on only
one thing in the end. They do not vote on whether you knew Kim Dotcom before or
after a certain date—they do not vote on this. They actually vote on one simple thing:
“Is this Government taking the place in the right direction, and will my family and so on
be better off with it, or is it tired, bored, arrogant, and out of touch, and it is time to kick
it out?”.
1586 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
When the time for a change comes, you cannot withstand it. I have been on either
side of it. In 1990 National had only to show up to win. In fact, sadly, we won a whole
lot of seats we really should n ot have won, and we ended up with a few people who
were probably more trouble than they were worth. I think I am actually, sadly, on record
as calling them in this Chamber a bunch of dingbats, dipsticks, and dorks, and I regret
that—I regret it immensely. But we did have a huge win in 1990, and we did not need to
promise anything; we just had to show up, because the Labour Party in 1990 was in
complete freefall, imploding, and gone. But I have been on the other side of it. I can tell
you that in 1999 I used to go up to Premier House and sit with Jenny Shipley at night
thinking about what we would try to do as part of the campaign to reinvigorate where
we were. And guess what! Every day we announced the next thing, thinking that would
be it, and the next night we found we had dropped two more points in the polls, because
the time for a change had come and you just cannot fight against that tsunami as it
comes.
That is how simple it is. What attracts the public to whether it is time for this lot to
be swiped out or not is their own self -interest. It is the things they talk about around the
breakfast table. So Andrew Little is quite right to focus on whether taxpayers’ money
should be going off to Skycity to give it a big subsidy to run some massive convention
centre, because that matters. Your ordinary members of the public will say “I don’t
actually like the idea of that.” I do not think that Steven Joyce, Bill English, or John
Key like the idea of it, based on the comments I have heard.
But if you want to stick to your knitting about things that matter, do not just suddenly
throw a grenade in there about Māori sovereignty. Because I can tell you —and I want
any other member in this House to tell me whether I am wrong. How many people have
raised that with them in their electorate over the last 3 years? How many people have
walked up to me in the Pakuranga shopping centre and said: “Until I hear you guys
firmly on the ground of some Māori sovereignty, so they can have some more control
over their rules and their laws and so on, I’m not voting for you again.”? Not one. Not a
sausage, not a mutter, not a murmur. So he just blew all of his good work, and it was not
actually that good. He was a better leader than anybody else Labour has had, because he
was not making m istakes or slipping up, but my message to the Labour Party is that
when your time comes it comes and when it does not you are wasting your time.
Think about big brands. Microsoft controlled the world for about 15 years and no one
could touch it. When Steve Jobs came back to Apple it was 90 days away from
insolvency and being put into bankruptcy —just about gone. And now it is poor old
Microsoft that cannot come up with a new product that anyone wants. Vista was a
disaster, Windows 8 did not work, or Windows  8.1. It has even scrapped Windows 9. It
is going to go straight to Windows 10, and it still cannot make it, and the company that
was insolvent called Apple is now booming and it is the richest company in the world.
Because the public like the brand, they like where it is going, and they are not going to
change.
So my message to the Labour Party is simply this —and this is really aimed at a
couple of people. First of all, Andrew Little and his Māori sovereignty —but to hear
Jacinda Ardern today using question time to talk about the National Library changing
from the book- based system to an internet -based system, and making more stuff
available online. I mean, for God’s sake, this is like the candle industry being upset
when electricity and lightbulbs were sta rting to come in. The National Library needs
changing like you would not believe, to come into the 21 st century, and maybe stop off
at the 19th and 20th along the way. And here she is using question time to raise an issue
that not one person has raised.
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1587
So the message to Labour is this. This Government has taken the country in the right
direction for 6 years, the public like it, but we must never take that for granted, because
they could easily, easily decide within no time at all you lot are gone. But rig ht now,
Labour had better get its act together, because it looks so dishevelled and is pointing in
so many different directions. There is a word for it, emanating from the centre, pointing
in all directions: quaquaversal.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: First, I will have to welcome all of my
esteemed colleagues back for 2015. Congratulations, Mr Assistant Speaker, to you as
well. In New Zealand First, we are really looking forward to this year, when the people
of New Zealand are going to be put first. We are in this circadian rhythm that Maurice
Williamson was talking about—raring to go, raring to go. However, when we were
listening to the Prime Minister’s statement, we were quite surprised to hear that there
was not a mention of health. Where is the importance that is being given to health? The
only mention that we heard was free health care for the under -13s. Well, I will have to
inform the House that that happens to have been a New Zealand First policy. We know
that imitation is the most sincere form of flattery, and particularly in this House. That
happens to have been a New Zealand First policy that is going to be implemented, so we
welcome the Government looking through our other policies and act ually putting those
into practice as well.
The policy that we are really hoping the Government is going to pick up on—and we
actually know it will—is three free doctors’ visits for all SuperGold cardholders. Well,
that will really save the Government some  money. We will pick up illnesses at a very
early stage, and before people go into hospital, they will have been cured by their GP.
We know, on this side of the House, that many SuperGold cardholders have great
trouble going to the doctor and paying for the doctor. This would be one way of getting
them there. We get many complaints about people going to hospital in an ambulance —
although their going to hospital is a good thing—and when they are told to go at 1
o’clock or 2 o’clock in the morning, they cannot  get home. This is a big issue when it
comes to senior citizens, so that is a great initiative, and we look forward to that
initiative being implemented this year too. I think it is rather odd that the Prime Minister
did not talk about the health of New Ze alanders, so we will be listening very carefully
again when it comes to the Budget, because on this side of the House we know it is
important.
We were very pleased to hear the Prime Minister talking about jobs and job creation.
We know that is quite fantas tic, but the reality is that there are a lot of people out there
who are having great difficulties even getting out of bed to find these jobs because of
illness or disability, and, consequently, they are living on the poverty line. Although we
have the Pri me Minister wanting us to believe that the health of all New Zealanders is
rosy, we know that it is really anything but. We need to focus in this area.
We have many New Zealanders who have fronted up to the hospital, to have their
operations cancelled time and time ag ain. They are on the waiting list, they go in, and
they are sent home again. That is not helping them one scrap. We know it is happening;
we are told of many instances of this. Why are so many Kiwis struggling with pain and
discomfort? We know that the number of cancelled elective surgeries has reduced since
2008. It is absolutely disgraceful and it is not how it should be. We look at the loss of
their earnings, we look at their mental fatigue, and it is something that needs addressing.
We are keen, on this side of the House, particularly in New Zealand First, to see some
action in this particular area.
Another issue that Kiwis have is cancer. We all wonder how on earth we can deal
best with this terrible disease. The New Zealand Breast Cancer Fo undation has called
for an increase in free mammograms for females until the age of 74. It is presently 69,
1588 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015
and we would like to see it increased to 74. We know that the risk of breast cancer
increases quite markedly as people age, and we all want somethin g done. Screening
does save lives. Over in Australia they have screening until the age of 74, so why can
we not have it here? But there is good news. We have been carefully following the
bowel cancer screening programme that is currently being carried out in Waitematā. It is
very successful, and we had the Hon Jo Goodhew say:“ … results for the first two years
of the programme show that most of the cancers were found at an early stage, when they
can often be cured,”.
So why is the Government waiting until 2 016 before even thinking about
implementing a national screening programme? How many more lives are going to be
needlessly lost when bowel cancer can be cured if it is caught at an early stage? The
trial says unequivocally that it works, and we heard that at an annual review this week,
when we looked at the Waitematā District Health Board. It works in Australia, it works
up in Waitematā, it works in the United Kingdom—why can it not work in the rest of
New Zealand? I believe it can. Instead, we are going to  have to wait for more people to
die before the Government is actually going to make this cancer a priority issue.
Another cancer that is really sort of a challenge is skin cancer and melanoma.
Overseas, over in Australia, although the skin cancer rate may be higher, the survival
rate is far higher from melanoma and skin cancer. We know that using sunbeds actually
increases the risk of skin cancer by 41 percent. Fortunately, we have now got some
legislation to regulate this particular issue to have a look at and to put through the
House through the Health Committee. We know that the voluntary guidelines are being
dragged out and are not really being followed through by many of the tanning clinics,
and there is no wish to do anything else. Why have we not got the under -18s banned
from actually using these facilities? This is not putting the lives of New Zealanders first.
Another issue that we are increasingly concerned about is that of obesity.
Unfortunately, New Zealanders are getting bigger and bigger, and their waistlines are
expanding—this is not the most healthy development. It actually puts stress and
pressure on the health system. I have got some figures here.

12 Feb 2015 Business Statement 1535 
 
THURSDAY, 12 FEBRUARY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : My apologies for being late 
and holding up the House for a minute. I was, of course, speaking to media outside, a 
phenomenon not known to my opponents on the other side of the House—[Interruption] 
Unless they are talking about each other, then they are pretty good. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE : When the House resumes on Tuesday, 17 Februar y 
the Government will look to progress the debate on the Prime Minister’ s statement and 
a number of pieces of legislation on the Order Paper, including the Gambling 
Amendment Bill (No 2), the Parole Amendment Bill, and the Energy (Fuels , Levies, 
and References) Amendment Bill. 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Senior Whip—Labour) : Can I just check with the Leader of 
the House that it is his exp ectation that there will be a members ’ day the week after 
next? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : Unless there are some 
unforeseen circumstances, that is the plan. 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economy—Reports 
1. CHRIS BISHOP (National) to the Minister of Finance: What recent reports has 
he received about what progress the Government is making to support more jobs and 
higher incomes? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the  Minister 
of Finance : I have seen several reports, particularly since this House last sat before 
Christmas, confirming that the growing economy is continuing to support more jobs and 
higher incomes. For example, Statistics New Zealand last week reported that in the past 
year another 80,000 jobs were created across New Zealand. The labour market 
participation rate increased to a record 69.7 percent, and unemployment, at 5.7 percent, 
is lower than i n most other developed economies. Average weekly wages rose 2.5 
percent in the calendar year of 2014, compared with consumer price inflation of just 0.8 
percent in the same period, and we also now know that mortgage interest rates will stay 
lower for longe r. So the growing economy is helping New Zealanders in many ways, 
but, of course, there is always more work to do to lock in those gains over the longer 
term. 
Chris Bishop : In light of forecasts of further strong economic growth, what is the  
outlook for inflation and interest rates? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Both inflation and interest rate pressures are low, and they 
are expected to remain that way now for the foreseeable future. The Reserve Bank noted

Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister of Local Government) : What a fantastic 
country we live in, and what a fantastic bunch of New Zealanders we have got in it. We 
have just had a fantastic summer. We have got so many things on track. We have more 
work to do, but we are heading in the right direction. 
Let us look at the fact that we have got one of the highest economic growth rates in 
the OECD. Employment is growing, with 80,000 new jobs created last year. Fewer 
people are dependent on welfare. The 2014 December quarter shows that benefit 
numbers are at a 6 -year low. We have fewer teens having babies than we have had in 
the last 42 years. We are seeing our roads being upgraded. More New Zealanders are 
getting the operations they need. We are seeing our construction centre booming. More  
houses are getting built. That is the reality of the direction this country is going in. 
However, if you listen to the Opposition, you would think it is all doom and gloom. 
It might be in their lives—it might be in their lives. That might be how it is for Labour. I 
mean, if you do not like the person you are sitting next to and if only four of you 
actually voted for the leader that you have got, then it might be that it is a bit doom and 
gloom. But that is not the reality of the New Zealand that we are living in today. It is not 
the reality of what we are seeing in the lives that people are living, in the optimism they 
have, and in the belief not only that through their own hard work things are getting 
better but also that the future looks pretty damned bright. 
This year we have announced, though, a fundamental policy within the housing and 
social housing sector so that we can continue to make sure we are addressing the needs 
of New Zealanders who really need help the most. For years we have seen Labour 
trying to define whether or not New Zealanders are getting their housing needs met by 
counting the number of houses that the State owns —full stop. There is no consideration 
given to the lives that those people are leading and the support services that they mig ht 
actually need. There is no consideration given to whether or not there might actually be 
someone better than the State who could do a better job for them. Let us just count the 
houses, tick that box, and we have done our job, which, by the way, would ge t kind of 
interesting in itself if we did decide to go down that track, because Labour had only 
59,000 houses back in 2004, and we now lease up to 69,000—but we will not let the 
facts get in the way of Labour’s doom and gloom story. 
So we announced changes  that mean, fundamentally, that New Zealanders will have 
more choice, more availability of social housing, and better services wrapped around 
them as individuals, and we are growing a community housing sector that  is, quite 
frankly, awesome —awesome; absolutely incredible. There is someone in this House 
who agrees with me. You heard me in question time today. It is quite exciting. Phil 
Twyford himself —yes, Phil Twyford himself —goes out there and says to the 
community housing sector: “We are committed to your  members having access to the 
income-related rents subsidy, to capital grants, and to stock transfer.” Well tick, tick, 
tick—that is actually Government policy. Thanks for the support, Phil Twyford. Good 
on you! But, members, you would be mistaken if you thought that he was actually being 
consistent and that what he said to them is what he actually believed. That is not true. 
Just this week —in fact, just today —we got a crowdfunding email to Labour 
supporters. It says: “Can you imagine John Key’s face if he opened the newspaper next 
week and saw a full page ad highlighting how many New Zealanders are against State 
house sell-offs? He would be straight on the phone to his Ministers. Through the power 
of crowdfunding we can make that happen. We can put an ad in the paper—if only you

can all give us a couple of pennies, because we do not even actually have the money to 
put an ad in the paper.” So poor Labour, guys —it is heading for a by -election it cannot 
afford; it is flip -flopping on policy. It goes out to the community sector saying one

New Zeal anders who are stuck on these zero- hour contracts. What is a zero- hour 
contract? It is a contract where the worker has to make themselves available for work at 
all times, but there is no requirement whatsoever on the employer to provide that worker 
with work. They are, therefore, very different from casual contracts. Casual contracts 
can provide flexibility both for the employer and the employee, but it is an absolutely 
one-sided relationship with these zero- hour contracts, and we see more and more of 
them every day, particularly in the fast -food industry but also increasingly in 
supermarkets and in the retail industry. We know that we are just going to see more and 
more of them if the Government does not take action.

going to do about zero -hour contracts? The answer was nothing. There was not a 
mention of it —not one. So today I lodged my Employment Relations (Certainty at 
Work) Amendment Bill, which takes aim at zero -hour contracts and seeks to rule them 
out from our employment relations framework. So what will have to happen is that 
employers will have to give an indication of how many hours a worker can expect to get 
if they have to be available for work at all times. It still a llows flexibility—of course,

that they can plan, so that they can put food on the table  for their children every single 
week, so that they can go to the bank and talk about getting a loan or a mortgage, and so

got a job, you would be able to make ends meet, provide for your family, and get ahead.

and we are seeing them used more and more every day. This Government has 
completely ignored that issue.

is required to ensure that our Employment Relations Act ceases the use of these zero -

Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) : The Prime Minister’s statement on Tuesday 
was steady as she goes. Setting aside the ribald and irrelevant commentary that peppers 
his deliveries to the House these days, Mr Key strove to provide the usual reassurances 
to the New Zealand people: sound fiscal management, support for business 
entrepreneurship, State sector reform, and earthquake recovery. We have been on the 
receiving end of this for 5 years now. It has become a mantra; a form of hypnopaedia —
a National lullaby for those who wish to be reassured, to retire to bed secure in the 
knowledge that our nation is in good hands.  
There was no penetrating and insightful comment on the global situation. Let us 
consider what the Prime Minister had to say about the world out there. First, our tenure 
on the Security Council places us, he observed, “at the heart of international decision 
making.” New Zealand is determined, he said, to “effect real change” on the council. 
“We have,” he said, “already demonstrated our willingn ess to be a strong independent 
voice”. This comes a week after he advised the BBC, and thus the world, that 
contributing military training to Iraq is the price of the club. “Ultimately,” he told the 
world, “are we going to say we are going to be part of a club like [we] are with the Five 
Eyes intelligence? Are we ultimately going to be able to rely on members of those clubs 
to support us in our moment of need?”. Unless there be any uncertainly as to the nature 
of the club, the Prime Minister, drawing himself up to the full height of responsible 
global citizenship, added: “And we do know that, when it comes to the United States 
and Canada and Australia and Great Britain and others, that we can rely on them.” And 
what can we contribute? Well, not much, but a bit. He said: “Even if the contribution is 
small—of course it will be proportional —there has to be some contribution. It is the 
price of the club.”

The Prime Minister merged his BBC interview in London with a side trip to Davos, 
where his favourite club of clubs —the global business elite—tolerated his presence. He 
was accompanied there by his “Minister for Trade and Dangerous Climate Change”, 
Tim Groser, who said in the House last year that New Zealand was now being accepted 
in “the big boys’ club” through his personal participation in the G20 and the World 
Economic Forum. This kind of diplomacy titillates our national leader, fresh from 
Christchurch a spiration and London currency markets, where club membership is 
indeed the passport to financial and political power. As a result, 6 years into the John 
Key Government the nation’s foreign policy is characterised by a certain “clubbiness”. 
Congratulations and prizes to the nation’s two top club members.  
There is a self -evident contradiction—a logical mistake —being made here. We 
cannot say there has to be a contribution as the price of the club and then say we are 
independent. Not even my 10 -year-old granddaughter would buy that line, nor her 8-
year-old sister. They were not born yesterday. I am not sure about their 3- year-old 
cousin, but I would not want to subject the Prime Minister to his wrath, so I would 
advise him to think carefully before double -speaking to the sons and daughters of this 
country. The price of the club is the price of the club. That price is providing troops to 
war-torn and weary places in response to pressure from the leaders of the club, even 
when we are privately in doubt —even when w e say they are there for training. This is 
how the Americans kicked off in Viet Nam 50 years ago. And if we are frantically 
shoring up Iraq’s army today, has any club member asked the grand leader why it saw 
such wisdom and vision 12 years ago in dismantling it?  
I say to the Prime Minister that if you are an independent nation, you are not 
beholden to a club—never. You abide by binding decisions of the United Nations. That 
is being part of the human family. The so- called club, whose membership you value so 
highly and hold in such personal esteem, illegally invaded the very country you are 
sending our troops to again. The US, the UK, and Australia illegally invaded Iraq in 
2003. Some club! What to call it —the lawbreakers? And we did it ourselves once, 
before that. Back in 1956 we were torn between two members of our club: Britain and 
Australia on the one hand, and the leading club member, the United States, on the other.  
We sided with our closer cousins and invaded Egypt —also illegally. We got 
censured and condemned by the Security Council on behalf of the larger human family. 
We had to withdraw. It was a humiliating moment for the UK especially, signifying the 
end of its global leadership. So we have a bit of a track record in sloping along inside

A majority on the council, including three permanent members, opposed military

MATT DOOCEY (National —Waimakariri): Happy New Year, Mr Assistant 
Speaker Mallard, and happy New Year to my parliament ary colleagues. I am looking 
forward to a great year in 2015: a great year in the House, a great year in the region of 
Canterbury, and a great year in my electorate of Waimakariri.  
The Prime Minister started his excellent speech on Tuesday morning by talk ing 
about jobs. He talked about incomes, and he talked about supporting families. I went to 
hear the Salvation Army’s state of the nation report yesterday morning, and I was 
interested in the fact that during the presentation the organisation showed a line  graph 
that was tracking downwards, and that was child poverty. So, as the curious new, young 
MP I am, I put my hand up and I asked Alan Johnson, who wrote the report, why child 
poverty is tracking down. His response was: “Job creation.” There you go —job creation 
reduces child poverty, and this National Government has created 80,000 new jobs in the 
last year and will create 150,000 new jobs in the next 2 years. Can I remind the 
Opposition members that the last state of the nation report by the Salvation Arm y when 
they were in Government in 2008 said that for all their increased expenditure they did 
not increase social progress by 1 percent.  
The Prime Minister also spoke on Tuesday about the Canterbury earthquake 
recovery. The earthquake recovery is a big and key focus of mine, as I have a 
background in health, specifically in mental health. I am not talking just about bricks 
and mortar when I talk about recovery. International research will show us that years 3 
to 5 are the most problematic for psychological and social recovery, and I think we need 
to remind ourselves that it is not the Christchurch earthquake and rebuild; it is the 
Canterbury earthquakes and rebuild. A town in my electorate, Kaiapoi, was hit severely 
by the first earthquakes in September 2010. So I would like to remind people about the 
Canterbury District Health Board’s All Right? campaign. It is worth repeating that it is 
all right to ask for help, and I would ask my parliamentary colleagues to ensure we 
continue to focus on the Canterbury e arthquake recovery in 2015 and provide the 
support that Cantabrians need.  
The year 2015 is going to be a great year of milestones and new beginnings in 
Canterbury. I opened last month, with the Mayor of Waimakariri, David Ayers, the 
Ruataniwha Kaiapoi Civic Centre, which has a new library of 30,000 books, a museum, 
and an art space. It was built using technology that will see the building last well into 
the future. It is a good example of local and central government working together with 
the local communi ty to build an anchor project that is a symbol of recovery and a 
symbol of the way we are heading in the future. I am proud to be part of a Government 
that believes in community facilities, strong families, and caring communities. The 
Government gave a grant to the Waimakariri District Council of $7 million, and $1.5 
million of that was used towards this new library development. The year 2015 is going 
to be a great year of milestones and new beginnings in the Canterbury earthquake 
recovery. In the next mont h we will open the Rangiora and Oxford town halls. We will 
open the Ashley Bridge. The North Canterbury Health Hub will open up in the middle 
of the year, and my constituents are looking forward to first -class health care facilities 
on their doorstep. We w ill be starting $300 million of roading projects, which will 
reduce commuter congestion, and the future use of red-zoned land will be decided.  
But tonight the eyes of the world will be on Christchurch with the International 
Cricket Council  Cricket World C up opening. At the start of the year I watched the 
Black Caps beat Sri Lanka at the new Hagley Oval, and it was impressive as I watched 
the crowd—because Cantabrians love their sport. It was a hot nor’wester day and they 
were enjoying this new sporting fac ility. It was great to see one of the Canterbury

anchor recovery projects being so successful, and now we have, arguably, the best 
cricket ground in New Zealand.  
Can I say that the Government is continuing to stand beside the people of Canterbury 
as good progress is made on the earthquake rebuild. The year 2015 is going to be a year 
of milestones and new beginnings in the Canterbury recovery. Thank you. 
NUK KORAKO (National) : Tēnā koe, e te Mana Whakawā. I rise to support the 
motion, but, firstly, I want to acknowledge the passing of two great leaders of 
Māoridom: Apirana Mahuika of Ngati Porou and Tama Huata of Ngāti Kahungunu. Nō 
reira, e ngā rakatira haere atu rā, haere atu  rā. Haere atu rā ki te pao o te whakawairua, 
takoto mai, takoto. [ And so, to the esteemed elders, go forth; farewell. Depart to the 
spiritual beat. Lie there, rest.] Let the dead be the dead and the living be the living. 
I want to highlight one thing that  the Prime Minister said in his speech: National is a 
Government doing something for Māori. One of the reasons I sought to enter Parliament 
as a National MP was to advance the cause of Māori. Some of my people have 
expressed scepticism and asked how I coul d join National. These are the people who 
buy in to the widespread perception that the party opposite is the one that can do the 
most for our people. Let me be clear. I joined the National Party because it is the party 
that has done the most for Māori in the past and will do the most for Māori in the future. 
It is indeed about aspirations. For too long Māori have been at the bottom of many 
major social indicators —in particular, education and welfare dependency. For too long 
Māori have looked for Labour to t urn things round. For too long Labour has let our 
people down. 
Labour is full of rhetoric on the importance of education. From what I have seen and 
heard, the Māori MPs on the other side of the House really care about our people and 
the importance of a good education. They talk a good game, but when it comes time to 
stand up and do something about the problems that exist, it is the teachers unions that 
get the final say. Labour’s answers to educational underachievement have been to 
ignore the failing schools, to oppose telling parents how their children are doing, and to 
fight against innovation in our education system. Our whānau want their kids to 
succeed. So when National says we should help parents to be more involved in their 
child’s learning, they welc ome that. They welcome being told in plain language how 
their children are doing. They welcome having data available that shows how their 
children’s school is performing. They agree with the Government that schools should be 
operating in the interests of their students and not those of the teachers union bosses. 
The fact that National is good for Māori is evident from the settlement of historic 
Treaty claims. As the Prime Minister said in his speech, Labour signed only one or two 
deeds of settlement per year. But now, just after over 6 years of a National Government, 
we have signed 46 deeds of settlement. That is fantastic progress and it makes me proud 
to represent National. 
I want to acknowledge our relationship with the Māori Party. Together, we have 
improved social outcomes for Māori through Whānau Ora, and we have repealed Helen 
Clark’s land -grab of the foreshore and seabed. This Government remains relentlessly 
focused on lifting the living standards of Māori, along with every other New Zealander, 
through economic growth. Labour’s approach to Māori in poverty has been to keep 
them there. Labour talks about jobs and lifting our people out of poverty, and when the 
time has come to act, it has done nothing. On this side of the House we know what it 
takes to lift people out of poverty. It is not sitting around talking about what a job is. It 
is not voting against every single job -creating measure this Government has put in 
place. It is not burdening small businesses with red tape and higher taxes and still 
expecting them to take on one more staff member. 
1580 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015 
 
National has restored confidence in our economy, which was crippled by the global 
recession and a Labour Government. Businesses now have the confidence to take on 
new workers thanks to the 90- day trial period. As I said at the beginning of my speech,

I live on a papatupu, or an ancestral community. This is the Māori heartland. I can

Dr PARMJEET PARMAR (National) : It is with pleasure that I rise to take part in 
this debate on the Prime Minister’s statement. I am really proud to be part of t his team 
in Government, because when the National -led Government presented its first Budget, 
in 2009, it did so against the backdrop of a sharp recession that began in early 2008 and 
the impact of the worst global financial crisis since the 1930s. In the a bsence of policy 
change, the outlook was going to be endless debt and exploding levels of Government 
debt. On top of this, New Zealand experienced the Canterbury earthquakes and a series 
of finance company failures.  
So the Government’s plan throughout thi s period was to support the economy in the 
short term by running operating deficits, reflecting lower tax revenue and higher 
spending on items such as benefits. This approach of the Government provided that 
extra support to the economy when it was needed t he most, and cushioned New 
Zealanders and their families in the recession when this was required. However, the 
Government did so within a clear framework of helping Kiwis get ahead and getting net 
Government debt below 20 percent by 2020. Now, our GDP grow th is among the 
highest in the OECD, and is expected to average almost 3 percent over the next 5 years.  
New Zealand is doing well compared with most other countries. Interest rates are 
staying lower for longer. Household disposable income is rising faster  than inflation, 
rising by 9 percent in real terms in the last 4 years, and is forecast to increase by another 
9 percent over the next 4 years. Unemployment is forecast to drop to 4.5 percent by 
2018. Employment is growing. Yes, employment is growing. Eighty thousand more 
people are employed than a year ago, and 217,000 more people are employed than 5 
years ago. This Government knows how to create the environment where businesses can 
prosper and have the confidence of investing more in their businesses and employing 
more staff. New Zealand recorded 3.9 percent economic growth over the year to June, 
which was one of the higher rates among developed countries.  
The New Zealand economy provides an amazing opportunity for businesses and 
investments. The investme nt opportunities are endless. New Zealand is recognised 
globally as being a safe place to invest and do business. We are growing new industries, 
such as information and communications technology and high- tech manufacturing, and 
strengthening existing ones, such as the food industry, tourism, and international 
education. And we are making strides in areas such as welfare, education, health, and 
law and order, to help improve the lives of New Zealanders and their families. I cannot

JONO NAYLOR (Natio nal): Can I say that it is exciting to be associated with a 
Government that is getting on and getting things done. I found it kind of interesting to 
hear from the last speaker from the opposite benches, who decided she would try to 
accuse us of dropping the ball, yet at the last election ours was not the party that 
dropped a seat. In fact, ours was a party that actually grew. And why did we grow? 
Well, we grew, in terms of the majority that we had, because New Zealanders liked 
what they saw over the last 6 years. They liked what this Government was doing and 
they wanted more of it. They saw that there was something that they could be confident 
in, and so they returned this National Government to the Treasury benches.  
And why did they do it? Well, I can tell  you that the people I speak to on the streets 
every day in Palmerston North have told me that it is because they have got confidence 
in this Government and they have got confidence in this Prime Minister and in the 
Minister of Finance. They have proved themselves worthy of the trust of the people of 
New Zealand because they are getting things moving and New Zealand is improving. 
But our work here is not finished. There is more for us to do. Although we are not 
making Mainland cheese, good things do take some time, so we will continue to work 
hard to continue to progress to ensure that New Zealand is moving forward.  
There have been calls from the opposite side, as we have been talking about social 
housing, that we should simply leave it alone. Well, I want to tell you a story from my 
experiences in Palmerston North to explain just exactly why we should not leave social 
housing alone. Last year, while campaigning, during the campaign, I was speaking to 
somebody down at the markets —at the Albert Street Market,  in fact—who told me that 
she was a Housing New Zealand tenant and had been in her house for about 30 years. I 
thought “Well, that’s good.” She clearly needed the assistance of the New Zealand 
people to be able to remain in that house. She said that she was income tested and so she 
had to pay only $80 a week for her house. I thought “Well, if that’s her situation and 
what she can afford, then perhaps it’s appropriate that that’s what she pays.” She told 
me that her children had left home and that she was now living in her four -bedroom 
1582 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015 
 
house. But do not worry; those rooms were not going to waste, because those rooms 
were being occupied by overseas students, who were paying board to this person. 
It was all above board, to be honest, because if you have two boa rders you do not 
have to declare the income. In fact, you could argue that it was very entrepreneurial on 
her part. But actually, as I was talking to her, I could not help but think of the stories 
that we are all told and we hear about and have come across , of families with three or 
more children who are perhaps living in overcrowded conditions because there is not 
enough housing for them or appropriate housing for them to occupy. I thought perhaps 
they would make better use of that house than international  students lining the pockets 
of somebody who was, to be fair, making a profit on the back of hard- working New 
Zealanders who are paying taxes and who are, perhaps, more deserving of that house. 
Although I am not saying that we should just simply evict people from those houses, we 
do need to engage more with them and ensure that we are monitoring them, and looking 
to ensure that the resources that we have for our social housing in New Zealand are 
actually being used in the most appropriate way.  
Yesterday Ho using New Zealand came to the Social Services Committee to talk 
about the year in review. It is very clear that we have got greater demand for certain 
types of housing in certain places around New Zealand and less demand in other places. 
Therefore, it is time something was done to rectify to that. So that is what we are doing. 
That is what our Minister for Social Housing is doing. She has outlined her plans to do 
that. She has outlined that we are not simply going to put people in houses and leave 
them alone for 30 years. We are going to look for new ways to manage this. We are 
going to engage with community organisations, which might, perhaps, for this person 
have moved her on to a point where she did not need social housing any more.  
So we have a plan. We  are going to support more New Zealanders into housing that 
meets their needs. We are going to ensure that they can start to move towards 
independence. We are going to increase the affordable housing supply, particularly in 
Auckland. We have got a plan. We  are working towards it. New Zealand will be the 
better for another 3 years of this National Government.

Hon JUDITH COLLINS (National —Papakura): Can I start the year by saying 
happy New Year to everyone—all our parliamentary colleagues and yourself, Mr 
Assistant Speaker.  
Su’a William Sio: Happy New Year, Judith. 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS : Thank you very much. I have to say that after that 
blistering attack from the member who has just resumed his seat, I should be feeling 
some trepidation, but I am going to overcome that in the spirit of Parliament.

interrupting the member —and I will start her time again —but I am meant to say that 
this is a split call. It is a 5-minute speech. 
Hon Maurice Williamson: We’re a split personality. 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS : Ha, ha! Yes, we are splitting this with my colleague the 
Hon Maurice Williamson, which I think is so appropriate. 
Well, we have started the year quite interestingly. I think one of the great things in 
the speeches from the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition was the tone. 
Actually, Mr Andrew Little has been leader of the Labour Party for a matter of a few 
months, and he was actually doing OK before Christmas. He was doing so OK that 
many in the media were writing him up as the next best thing, and I am sure Labour 
thought that it had finally found someone it could support. [ Interruption] Well, he was 
pretty much the only other person standing who had not put their name up for some sort 
of role, and the real leader of the Labour Party, the Hon Annette King, was not available 
to take on the title. 
But, having said that, what happened to him? He got a rush of blood to the head, and 
I have been wondering why he would have started talking about Māori s overeignty and 
getting everybody excited. Certainly, in Papakura people are concerned about this new 
separatist movement that he seems to be wanting to promote. I thought: “What has gone 
wrong with Andrew Little?”, because I am actually quite fond of him—no, I really am; I 
am always fond of leaders of the Opposition because I think it is a good opportunity for 
them to show their stripes, and it is good to do that —and I have worked it out: it is the 
circadian rhythms. I did not know about circadian rhythms until Mr Little gave his first 
media interview after he became the Leader of the Opposition, and he was late. He was 
late because he does not believe in alarm clocks because of his circadian rhythms. So I 
guess on Waitangi Day his circadian rhythms were a b it out because he had to get up 
early. 
I have got a bit of news for him, and it is that if he wants to be the leader of this 
country, he is going to have to work out his circadian rhythms, because you cannot get 
up at 5 o’clock in the morning and then go a nd talk about Māori sovereignty and 
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1585 
 
separatism and think that the people of New Zealand are going to think that that is a 
good idea. I can tell you that Papakura is just all agog with it. I have to say that I am 
going to talk a bit more about that in Papak ura over the next 3 years, and I think quite a 
few people on this side of the House are going to help Mr Little remember the circadian 
rhythms and why he should be focused on the things that are actually important for 
Kiwis. 
One of the things that is reall y important—which the Prime Minister spoke about, 
and I have ad nauseam spoken and written about —is the need for Resource 
Management Act reform. When I was practising law, before the Resource Management 
Act even came in—oh, I know, I was a child genius! I know, Mr Assistant Speaker, that 
you do not believe for a moment that I could be that old. But, yes, I was practising law 
even when you were first an MP. I remember when the Resource Management Act 
came in. It was almost like a light had come on. What happ ened is all these town 
planners—who were then town planners —these fabulously experienced people, seemed 
to leave Auckland City and go out as consultants. That is what I was dealing with a lot. 
That is when we should always get concerned —when legislation le ads a lot of very 
experienced, good, hard-working, skilled people to suddenly leave their jobs to become 
consultants. That tells us there is something going on. So when we try to set up these 
sorts of systems—I think with all the best of intentions—it unfortunately becomes a real 
muddle. 
I had that experience just last year when getting some work done at our home in 
Maraetai. Many people will know about it; it has been on Campbell Live . They had a 
good look through my wardrobe, which I felt was mildly invas ive, but there you go. 
What we found was that with our little bridge, our walkway, we spent more money on 
resource consent than we did on building the bridge. I think, unfortunately, that that is 
just a little tale, but, actually, that is what is happening . We need to free up land, we 
need to free up people to make good decisions, and we actually need to be able to have 
faith in our builders and in the people who are developing land. One of the things in 
Auckland in particular—because that is where most of the issues are around housing —
is that it is really about this metropolitan urban limit, which was put in place about 15 
years ago. It has made it very expensive and difficult to actually get any new land 
brought in for housing, and it has been like that for about 10 or 15 years. This is what 
the developers are saying to me: “Sort this stuff out. Stop trying to impose limits on 
people and actually have some faith in them.” Thank you.

Collins has been talking about. I think that the rhythm method is obviously what Labour 
has been applying for some time. It is not working, and Labour needs to look for 
something else.  
I want to give Labour some advice. I have done this befo re, during drive time on 
Radio Live and so on, and Labour does not seem to listen to that, but I am going to do it 
again. It is really simple —it is really simple. The voting public actually vote on only 
one thing in the end. They do not vote on whether you knew Kim Dotcom before or 
after a certain date—they do not vote on this. They actually vote on one simple thing: 
“Is this Government taking the place in the right direction, and will my family and so on 
be better off with it, or is it tired, bored, arrogant, and out of touch, and it is time to kick 
it out?”.  
1586 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015 
 
When the time for a change comes, you cannot withstand it. I have been on either 
side of it. In 1990 National had only to show up to win. In fact, sadly, we won a whole 
lot of seats we really should n ot have won, and we ended up with a few people who 
were probably more trouble than they were worth. I think I am actually, sadly, on record 
as calling them in this Chamber a bunch of dingbats, dipsticks, and dorks, and I regret 
that—I regret it immensely. But we did have a huge win in 1990, and we did not need to 
promise anything; we just had to show up, because the Labour Party in 1990 was in 
complete freefall, imploding, and gone. But I have been on the other side of it. I can tell 
you that in 1999 I used to go up to Premier House and sit with Jenny Shipley at night 
thinking about what we would try to do as part of the campaign to reinvigorate where 
we were. And guess what! Every day we announced the next thing, thinking that would 
be it, and the next night we found we had dropped two more points in the polls, because 
the time for a change had come and you just cannot fight against that tsunami as it 
comes.  
That is how simple it is. What attracts the public to whether it is time for this lot to 
be swiped out or not is their own self -interest. It is the things they talk about around the 
breakfast table. So Andrew Little is quite right to focus on whether taxpayers’ money 
should be going off to Skycity to give it a big subsidy to run some massive convention 
centre, because that matters. Your ordinary members of the public will say “I don’t 
actually like the idea of that.” I do not think that Steven Joyce, Bill English, or John 
Key like the idea of it, based on the comments I have heard. 
But if you want to stick to your knitting about things that matter, do not just suddenly 
throw a grenade in there about Māori sovereignty. Because I can tell you —and I want 
any other member in this House to tell me whether I am wrong. How many people have 
raised that with them in their electorate over the last 3 years? How many people have 
walked up to me in the Pakuranga shopping centre and said: “Until I hear you guys 
firmly on the ground of some Māori sovereignty, so they can have some more control 
over their rules and their laws and so on, I’m not voting for you again.”? Not one. Not a 
sausage, not a mutter, not a murmur. So he just blew all of his good work, and it was not 
actually that good. He was a better leader than anybody else Labour has had, because he 
was not making m istakes or slipping up, but my message to the Labour Party is that 
when your time comes it comes and when it does not you are wasting your time.  
Think about big brands. Microsoft controlled the world for about 15 years and no one 
could touch it. When Steve Jobs came back to Apple it was 90 days away from 
insolvency and being put into bankruptcy —just about gone. And now it is poor old 
Microsoft that cannot come up with a new product that anyone wants. Vista was a 
disaster, Windows 8 did not work, or Windows  8.1. It has even scrapped Windows 9. It 
is going to go straight to Windows 10, and it still cannot make it, and the company that 
was insolvent called Apple is now booming and it is the richest company in the world. 
Because the public like the brand, they like where it is going, and they are not going to 
change.  
So my message to the Labour Party is simply this —and this is really aimed at a 
couple of people. First of all, Andrew Little and his Māori sovereignty —but to hear 
Jacinda Ardern today using question time to talk about the National Library changing 
from the book- based system to an internet -based system, and making more stuff 
available online. I mean, for God’s sake, this is like the candle industry being upset 
when electricity and lightbulbs were sta rting to come in. The National Library needs 
changing like you would not believe, to come into the 21 st century, and maybe stop off 
at the 19th and 20th along the way. And here she is using question time to raise an issue 
that not one person has raised.  
12 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1587 
 
So the message to Labour is this. This Government has taken the country in the right 
direction for 6 years, the public like it, but we must never take that for granted, because 
they could easily, easily decide within no time at all you lot are gone. But rig ht now, 
Labour had better get its act together, because it looks so dishevelled and is pointing in 
so many different directions. There is a word for it, emanating from the centre, pointing 
in all directions: quaquaversal. 
BARBARA STEWART (NZ First) : First, I will have to welcome all of my 
esteemed colleagues back for 2015. Congratulations, Mr Assistant Speaker, to you as 
well. In New Zealand First, we are really looking forward to this year, when the people 
of New Zealand are going to be put first. We are in this circadian rhythm that Maurice 
Williamson was talking about—raring to go, raring to go. However, when we were 
listening to the Prime Minister’s statement, we were quite surprised to hear that there 
was not a mention of health. Where is the importance that is being given to health? The 
only mention that we heard was free health care for the under -13s. Well, I will have to 
inform the House that that happens to have been a New Zealand First policy. We know 
that imitation is the most sincere form of flattery, and particularly in this House. That 
happens to have been a New Zealand First policy that is going to be implemented, so we 
welcome the Government looking through our other policies and act ually putting those 
into practice as well.  
The policy that we are really hoping the Government is going to pick up on—and we 
actually know it will—is three free doctors’ visits for all SuperGold cardholders. Well, 
that will really save the Government some  money. We will pick up illnesses at a very 
early stage, and before people go into hospital, they will have been cured by their GP. 
We know, on this side of the House, that many SuperGold cardholders have great 
trouble going to the doctor and paying for the doctor. This would be one way of getting 
them there. We get many complaints about people going to hospital in an ambulance —
although their going to hospital is a good thing—and when they are told to go at 1 
o’clock or 2 o’clock in the morning, they cannot  get home. This is a big issue when it 
comes to senior citizens, so that is a great initiative, and we look forward to that 
initiative being implemented this year too. I think it is rather odd that the Prime Minister 
did not talk about the health of New Ze alanders, so we will be listening very carefully 
again when it comes to the Budget, because on this side of the House we know it is 
important. 
We were very pleased to hear the Prime Minister talking about jobs and job creation. 
We know that is quite fantas tic, but the reality is that there are a lot of people out there 
who are having great difficulties even getting out of bed to find these jobs because of 
illness or disability, and, consequently, they are living on the poverty line. Although we 
have the Pri me Minister wanting us to believe that the health of all New Zealanders is 
rosy, we know that it is really anything but. We need to focus in this area. 
We have many New Zealanders who have fronted up to the hospital, to have their 
operations cancelled time and time ag ain. They are on the waiting list, they go in, and 
they are sent home again. That is not helping them one scrap. We know it is happening; 
we are told of many instances of this. Why are so many Kiwis struggling with pain and 
discomfort? We know that the number of cancelled elective surgeries has reduced since 
2008. It is absolutely disgraceful and it is not how it should be. We look at the loss of 
their earnings, we look at their mental fatigue, and it is something that needs addressing. 
We are keen, on this side of the House, particularly in New Zealand First, to see some 
action in this particular area. 
Another issue that Kiwis have is cancer. We all wonder how on earth we can deal 
best with this terrible disease. The New Zealand Breast Cancer Fo undation has called 
for an increase in free mammograms for females until the age of 74. It is presently 69, 
1588 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2015 
 
and we would like to see it increased to 74. We know that the risk of breast cancer 
increases quite markedly as people age, and we all want somethin g done. Screening 
does save lives. Over in Australia they have screening until the age of 74, so why can 
we not have it here? But there is good news. We have been carefully following the 
bowel cancer screening programme that is currently being carried out in Waitematā. It is 
very successful, and we had the Hon Jo Goodhew say:“ … results for the first two years 
of the programme show that most of the cancers were found at an early stage, when they 
can often be cured,”. 
So why is the Government waiting until 2 016 before even thinking about 
implementing a national screening programme? How many more lives are going to be 
needlessly lost when bowel cancer can be cured if it is caught at an early stage? The 
trial says unequivocally that it works, and we heard that at an annual review this week, 
when we looked at the Waitematā District Health Board. It works in Australia, it works 
up in Waitematā, it works in the United Kingdom—why can it not work in the rest of 
New Zealand? I believe it can. Instead, we are going to  have to wait for more people to 
die before the Government is actually going to make this cancer a priority issue. 
Another cancer that is really sort of a challenge is skin cancer and melanoma. 
Overseas, over in Australia, although the skin cancer rate may be higher, the survival 
rate is far higher from melanoma and skin cancer. We know that using sunbeds actually 
increases the risk of skin cancer by 41 percent. Fortunately, we have now got some 
legislation to regulate this particular issue to have a look at and to put through the 
House through the Health Committee. We know that the voluntary guidelines are being 
dragged out and are not really being followed through by many of the tanning clinics, 
and there is no wish to do anything else. Why have we not got the under -18s banned 
from actually using these facilities? This is not putting the lives of New Zealanders first. 
Another issue that we are increasingly concerned about is that of obesity. 
Unfortunately, New Zealanders are getting bigger and bigger, and their waistlines are 
expanding—this is not the most healthy development. It actually puts stress and 
pressure on the health system. I have got some figures here.
